And this is the Book of our Lord, the Creator of all, the Provider of all, and the Originator of all, present among us, found in every house and in the hand of every Muslim, which has not been altered, changed, added to, diminished, distorted, or corrupted. We and you are among those who understand its words and grasp its meanings. So come, let us take the truth from its source and drink the pure water from its spring, for it is better guided than what you found your fathers upon." They say: "No hearing and no obedience," either by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of state. So reflect on this and consider it, if any remnant of fairness remains in you, a portion of goodness, a shred of modesty, and a share of religion. There is no power and no strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

I have explained this in the utmost clarity in my book which I named Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab. Refer to it if you wish that the darkness of partisanship be lifted from you and the clouds of taqlid be dispersed for you.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ — and that vengeance is what Allah inflicted upon the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud. ﴿So look how was the end of the deniers﴾ from those nations, for their traces are still present.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾ — that is: mention to them the time when he said to his father and his people, who imitated their fathers and worshipped idols: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. Al-Bara' ("free") is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective for emphasis, and it is used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine, and the feminine. Al-Jawhari said: "I disassociated myself from such-and-such, and I am free of it (bara' wa khala')," and it is not made dual or plural, because it is originally a masdar.

Then He excepted his Creator from the disassociation, so He said: ﴿Except He who originated me﴾, meaning: who created me, ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾, meaning: He will direct me to His religion and keep me firm upon the truth. The exception is either disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but He who originated me," or connected (muttasil), from the generality of ma ("what"), since they used to worship Allah and the idols together. His statement that He will certainly guide him reflects his firm trust in Allah, glorified is He, and the strength of his certainty.

﴿And He made it a word that remains in his posterity﴾. The pronoun in ja'alaha ("made it") refers to His saying: ﴿except He who originated me﴾, and it means monotheism, as if he said: "And He made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham, who are his descendants, so there will always be among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah, glorified is He." The subject of ja'alaha is Abraham, since he enjoined monotheism upon them and commanded them to adhere to it, as in His saying: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and so on. It has been said that the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, meaning: Allah, mighty and majestic is He, made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham. The ʿaqib ("posterity") means those who come after.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: the word is "There is no god but Allah," and there will always be from his posterity someone who worships Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Ikrimah said: it is Islam. Ibn Zayd said: the word is His saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. The clause ﴿so that they may return﴾ is a justification for the making (ja'l), meaning: He made it remain in hope that whoever among them associates partners with Allah would return to it by calling upon the One who affirms His oneness.

It has also been said that the pronoun in la'allahum ("so that they") refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: "so that the people of Makkah may return to your religion, which is the religion of Abraham."

It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended order is: "Indeed He will guide me, so that they may return, and He made it..." etc. Al-Suddi said: "so that they may repent, and thus return from what they are upon to the worship of Allah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned His favour upon Quraysh and those disbelievers of their time who agreed with them, so He said: ﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and to their fathers﴾. He turned away from the first speech to mention what He gave them enjoyment of, in souls, families, wealth, and kinds of blessings, and what He gave enjoyment of to their fathers, and He did not hasten punishment upon them. So they were deceived by the respite and devoted themselves to desires, ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning of mubin ("clear") is: manifest and clear in its message, or: one who makes clear to them what they need of the matters of religion. But they did not respond to him, nor did they act upon what was sent down to him.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear what they did when the truth came, so He said: ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."﴾ That is: deniers. So they called the Qur'an magic and denied it, and they belittled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?"﴾ By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if. By the two men is meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if, as Qatadah and others said. Mujahid and others said: ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah from Makkah and ʿUmayr ibn ʿAbd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. It has also been said otherwise.

The apparent sense of the wording is that the intended meaning is a man from one of the two towns, great in standing, wide in wealth, and a leader among his people. The meaning is: if it were a Qur'an, it would have been sent down upon a great man among the great ones of the two towns.

Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ meaning prophethood, or what is more general than it. The interrogative is for denial.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 2 of 2):

Then He (glorified is He) explained that it is He who apportioned among them the means of their livelihood in worldly affairs, so He said: ﴿It is We who apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾. He did not delegate that to them, and no one among the servants has the right to exercise authority over anything. Rather, judgement belongs to Allah alone. Since Allah (glorified is He) is the One who apportioned their provisions among them and raised some of them above others in rank, how then should they not be content with His apportioning in the matter of prophethood and His entrusting it to whomever He wills of His creation?

Muqatil said: He means, "Do they hold the keys of the Message, so that they place it wherever they wish?"

The majority of readers recited مَعِيشَتَهم (ma'ishatahum, "their livelihood") in the singular, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin recited مَعايِشَهم (ma'ayishahum, "their livelihoods") in the plural. The meaning of ﴿And We raised some of them above others in ranks﴾ is that He made distinctions among them, so that some were more excellent than others in worldly matters: in provision, leadership, strength, freedom, intellect and knowledge. Then He mentioned the reason for raising some of them in rank above others, saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾. That is, so that some may employ others: the wealthy employs the poor, the leader employs the subordinate, the strong employs the weak, the free employs the slave, the one of greater intellect employs the one below him in intellect, and the learned employs the ignorant. This holds in most circumstances of the people of this world, and by it their interests are fulfilled, their livelihood is organised, and each one of them attains what he seeks. For every worldly craft is practised well by one group and not by others, so some were made in need of others, so that consolation may be achieved among them in the enjoyment of worldly goods. This one needs that one, this one makes for that one, and this one gives to that one.

As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "We subjected" means "We gave them servants and attendants, so that the rich employ the poor, and thus some of them become a means of livelihood for others." Qatadah and ad-Dahhak said: "so that some may possess others." It has also been said that السُّخْرِيّ (sukhriyy) here is the sense of "mockery" (istihza'). Although this matches the lexical meaning, it is far from the meaning of the Qur'an and contrary to the intended context.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾. By "mercy" is meant what Allah has prepared for His righteous servants in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is prophethood, since it is what is meant by "mercy" in the earlier words: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾. There is no barrier to meaning by it everything that is called "mercy", either by inclusion or by substitution (badal). The phrase مِمّا يَجْمَعُونَ (mimma yajma'un, "than what they accumulate") means: what they accumulate of wealth and all the other goods of this world.

Then He (glorified is He) explained the insignificance of this world in His sight, so He said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾, that is, were it not that they would all gather in disbelief out of inclination toward this world and its adornment, ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver ceilings for their houses﴾. He used the plural pronoun in لِبُيُوتِهِمْ (libuyutihim, "for their houses") and the singular in يَكْفُرُ (yakfuru, "disbelieves") with regard to the meaning and the wording of مَن (man, "whoever"). لِبُيُوتِهِمْ is a بَدَل اشْتِمال (badal ishtimal, a substitution of inclusion) from the relative pronoun. السُّقُفُ (suqufun, "ceilings") is the plural of سَقْفٌ (saqf, "ceiling").

The majority recited سُقُفًا with a ḍammah on the sīn and the qāf, like رَهْنٌ and رُهُنٌ. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "There is no third form like them." Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of سَقِيفٌ (saqif), like كَثِيبٌ and كُثُبٌ, and رَغِيفٌ and رُغُفٌ. It has also been said that it is the plural of سُقُوفٌ (suquf), so it is a plural of a plural. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited سَقْفًا with a fatḥah on the sīn and a sukūn on the qāf, in the singular, and its meaning is plural because it is a generic noun (li-l-jins).

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is: were it not that people would all disbelieve because of their inclination toward this world and their leaving the Hereafter, We would have given them in this world what We have described, because of the insignificance of this world in the sight of Allah. Most of the exegetes held this view.

Ibn Zayd said: "Were it not that mankind would become one community" means, in the pursuit of this world and their preference for it over the Hereafter.

Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is: were it not that among the disbelievers there were rich and poor, and among the Muslims there were the same, We would have given the disbelievers of this world all of this, because of its insignificance. ﴿And staircases on which they ascend﴾. (p-1340) The مَعارِج (ma'arij) are the stairs, the plural of مِعراج (mi'raj), and the mi'raj is the ladder.

Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may make the singular مِعْرَجًا (mi'rajan) and مَعْرَجًا (ma'rajan), like مِرْقاةٌ and مَرْقاةٌ. The meaning is: We would have made for them staircases of silver, upon which they ascend, that is, they climb and ascend by means of the staircases. It is said: ظَهَرْتُ عَلى البَيْتِ (zahartu 'ala al-bayt, "I ascended onto the house"), meaning I rose to its roof. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"We reached the heavens in glory, honour and lordship, and indeed we hope for a higher ascent beyond that."

That is, a place to ascend.

﴿And doors for their houses, and couches on which they recline﴾. That is, We would have made for their houses doors of silver and couches of silver, ﴿on which they recline﴾. That is, on the couches, which is the plural of سَرِيرٌ (sarir). It has also been said it is the plural of أَسِرَّةٌ (asirrah), so it is a plural of a plural. الِاتِّكاء (al-ittika') and التَّوَكُّؤ (tawakkus) mean leaning heavily upon something, as in ﴿I lean upon it﴾ [Taha: 18], and one says اتَّكَأ عَلى الشَّيْءِ (ittaka'a 'ala al-shay'), so he is مُتَّكِئٌ (muttaki'), and the place is مُتَّكَأٌ (muttaka'). The زُخْرُف (zukhruf) is gold. It has also been said that it is adornment in general, whether gold or otherwise. Ibn Zayd said: it is what people make for their homes of furnishings and household goods. Al-Hasan said: it is decorative designs, and its root meaning is adornment; one says زَخْرَفْتُ الدّارَ (zakhraftu al-dar, "I adorned the house"), meaning I decorated it.

The accusative of زُخْرُفًا (zukhrufan) is either by a verb understood, meaning: "and We would have made for them, in addition to all that, adornment", or by removal of the preposition, meaning: "doors and couches of silver and of gold", and when the preposition is removed, the noun becomes accusative.

Then He (glorified is He) informed that all of that is only enjoyed in this world, so He said: ﴿And all that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. The majority recited لَمّا (lamma) with a light pronunciation, while 'Asim, Hamzah and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited it with the doubled mīm (lammā). On the first reading, إنْ (in) is the light form of the heavy إنَّ, and on the second reading it is a negation, and لَمّا has the sense of إلّا (illa, "except"), meaning: "all that is nothing but a thing enjoyed in this world."

Abu Raja' recited لِمّا with a kasrah on the lām, on the basis that the lām indicates cause and مّا is a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted: that is, for that which is an enjoyment.

﴿But the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾. That is, for whoever guards against polytheism and sins, believes in Allah alone and acts in obedience to Him, for it is the enduring one that does not perish, and its everlasting bounty does not cease.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿We found our fathers upon a community﴾: "upon a religion."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him concerning ﴿And He made it a word that remains﴾: "There is no god but Allah" in his posterity, and he said: "The posterity of Ibrahim, his son."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him, that he was asked about the saying of Allah ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾ "What are the two towns?" He said: "al-Ta'if and Makkah." It was said: "Who are the two men?" He said: "'Umayr ibn Mas'ud, and the best of the Quraysh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him: "By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if, and the great one is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Qurashi and Habib ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning the verse: "They mean: more honourable than Muhammad, [namely] al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from the people of Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from the people of al-Ta'if."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning His saying ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾ and the rest of the verse: "He says: Were it not that We would make all mankind disbelievers, We would have made for the houses of the disbelievers ceilings of silver, and staircases of silver, which are steps upon which they ascend to the upper rooms, and couches of silver, and zukhruf, which is gold."

At-Tirmidhi related it and authenticated it, and Ibn Majah related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single drink of water from it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ Am (أمْ) here is the disjunctive (al-munqati'a) "am," meaning "rather": "Did We give them a Book before the Qur'an, by which they worship other than Allah?" ﴿So they hold fast to it﴾ means they take up what is in it, argue by it, and make it a proof for themselves. It is also possible that am is a repetition of His saying "Did they witness their creation?", in which case it is connected (muttasila), and the meaning is: "Were they present at their creation, or have We given them a Book...?"

It has been said that the pronoun in min qablihi ("before this") refers to their claim, meaning: "Or have We given them a Book before their claim, which testifies to the soundness of what they claim?" The first view is preferable.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that they have no proof in their hands and no basis for doubt, but that they followed their fathers in misguidance. So He said: ﴿Nay, they say: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community (ummah), and indeed we are guided in their footsteps."﴾ Thus they acknowledged that they have no foundation except the blind imitation (taqlid) of their fathers. The meaning of ʿalā ummatin ("upon a community") is "upon a path and a creed." Abu ʿUbayd said: it is the path and the religion, and Qatadah and others said the same. Al-Jawhari said: the ummah is the path and the religion. It is said: "So-and-so has no ummah," meaning he has no religion and no sect. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"We were upon the ummah of our fathers, and we follow the first ones, the first ones."

And the saying of another:

"Is one who has an ummah equal to one who is ungrateful?"

Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: "upon a qiblah (direction of prayer)." Al-Akhfash said: "upon uprightness," and he recited the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I swore and I left no doubt for you, and does one who has an ummah sin while he is obedient?"

The majority read ummatin with a damma on the hamza (أُمَّةٍ). Mujahid, Qatadah, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz read it with a kasra (إِمَّةٍ).

Al-Jawhari said: al-immah (إِمَّة) with a kasra means "blessing," and al-immah is also a dialectal variant of al-ummah. From this is the saying of ʿAdi ibn Zayd:

"Then after prosperity and kingship and the ummah (al-umm-ah), the graves have buried them there."

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that others among the disbelievers before them had already reached this same statement and held it: ﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ Mutrafuha ("its affluent ones") means its wealthy and its leaders. Qatadah said: muqtadun means "following." The meanings of being guided (ihtida') and following (iqtida') are close, and He specified "the affluent" to draw attention to the fact that luxury is the cause of neglecting reflection.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them, so He said: ﴿He said: "Even if I brought you something better guiding than what you found your fathers upon?"﴾ That is: "Will you follow your fathers even if I bring you a religion better guided than the religion of your fathers?" Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Say to them: Will you follow what you found your fathers upon, even if I bring you something better than it?"

The majority read qul awa-law ji'tukum ("Say: even if I brought you"). Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read qala awa-law ji'tukum ("He said"). This is a narration of what took place between the warners and their peoples: each warner from those warners said to his community. It has also been said that both readings narrate what took place between the prophets and their peoples, as if it were said to each prophet: "Say," on the evidence of His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾

This is among the greatest proofs demonstrating the invalidity and ugliness of taqlid. These blind followers in Islam only act on the sayings of their predecessors, follow their traces, and imitate them. So when the one calling to the truth wishes to bring them out of misguidance or to repel them from an innovation which they have held fast to and inherited from their predecessors, without a clear proof or an evident argument, but merely by saying and what is said, with a false doubt, a worthless argument, and a baseless statement, they respond with what the affluent of these creeds said: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps,﴾ or with something whose meaning is close to that. If the one calling to the truth says to them: "The Islamic community has united us, and this Muhammadan religion has encompassed us, and Allah has not required us, nor you, nor your fathers before you, to worship except by His Book which He sent down to His Messenger, and by what is authentically related from His Messenger, for he is the one who makes clear the Book of Allah, clarifies its meanings, and distinguishes between its clear (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih) verses. So let us come and refer what we dispute to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, as Allah commanded us in His Book by His saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], for referring to them both is better guidance for us and for you than referring to what your predecessors said and what your fathers followed," they recoil like wild beasts and pelt the one calling them with every stone and clod, as if they had never heard the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ [al-Nur: 51], nor His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then they find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided, and they submit with full submission.﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]

If the one speaking says to them: "This scholar whom you imitate and whose sayings you follow is like you in that he is obligated to follow the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and is required to do what you are required to do. And when he acts by his own opinion because he does not find the evidence, that is a concession (rukhsah) for him, which it is not permissible for another to follow him in, nor lawful for him to act upon. Here I am, producing for you the evidence which he did not find, from the Book of Allah or from what is authentically established of the Sunnah of His Messenger, and that is better for you than what you found your fathers upon," they say: "We will not act on this, and there is no hearing and no obedience for you." They find in their hearts the greatest discomfort with the judgment of the Book and the Sunnah, and do not submit to it or accept it. Satan has given them a staff to lean on whenever they hear someone calling them to the Book and the Sunnah, which is that they say: "Our imam whom we imitated and followed knows the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger better than you do." This is because their minds have formed a great image of those whom they follow, due to the antiquity of the era and the multitude of followers. They do not realize that this claim is turned against them and repelled back into their faces. For if it were said to them: "There are among the Successors (tabi'un) those who are greater in rank and earlier in era than your companion. If antiquity of era and nobility of rank had a merit that necessitates following, then come, and I will show you one who is earlier in era and greater in rank." If they refuse that, then here I am, guiding you to one who is greater in rank, more eminent in standing, more numerous in followers, and earlier in era: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, our Prophet and your Prophet, the Messenger of Allah to us and to you. So come, for his Sunnah is present in the records and registers of Islam, which the whole of this community has received, generation after generation and era after era. And this is the Book of our Lord, the Creator of all, the Provider of all, and the Originator of all, present among us, found in every house and in the hand of every Muslim, which has not been altered, changed, added to, diminished, distorted, or corrupted. We and you are among those who understand its words and grasp its meanings. So come, let us take the truth from its source and drink the pure water from its spring, for it is better guided than what you found your fathers upon." They say: "No hearing and no obedience," either by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of state. So reflect on this and consider it, if any remnant of fairness remains in you, a portion of goodness, a shred of modesty, and a share of religion. There is no power and no strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

I have explained this in the utmost clarity in my book which I named Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab. Refer to it if you wish that the darkness of partisanship be lifted from you and the clouds of taqlid be dispersed for you.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ — and that vengeance is what Allah inflicted upon the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud. ﴿So look how was the end of the deniers﴾ from those nations, for their traces are still present.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾ — that is: mention to them the time when he said to his father and his people, who imitated their fathers and worshipped idols: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. Al-Bara' ("free") is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective for emphasis, and it is used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine, and the feminine. Al-Jawhari said: "I disassociated myself from such-and-such, and I am free of it (bara' wa khala')," and it is not made dual or plural, because it is originally a masdar.

Then He excepted his Creator from the disassociation, so He said: ﴿Except He who originated me﴾, meaning: who created me, ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾, meaning: He will direct me to His religion and keep me firm upon the truth. The exception is either disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but He who originated me," or connected (muttasil), from the generality of ma ("what"), since they used to worship Allah and the idols together. His statement that He will certainly guide him reflects his firm trust in Allah, glorified is He, and the strength of his certainty.

﴿And He made it a word that remains in his posterity﴾. The pronoun in ja'alaha ("made it") refers to His saying: ﴿except He who originated me﴾, and it means monotheism, as if he said: "And He made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham, who are his descendants, so there will always be among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah, glorified is He." The subject of ja'alaha is Abraham, since he enjoined monotheism upon them and commanded them to adhere to it, as in His saying: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and so on. It has been said that the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, meaning: Allah, mighty and majestic is He, made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham. The ʿaqib ("posterity") means those who come after.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: the word is "There is no god but Allah," and there will always be from his posterity someone who worships Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Ikrimah said: it is Islam. Ibn Zayd said: the word is His saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. The clause ﴿so that they may return﴾ is a justification for the making (ja'l), meaning: He made it remain in hope that whoever among them associates partners with Allah would return to it by calling upon the One who affirms His oneness.

It has also been said that the pronoun in la'allahum ("so that they") refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: "so that the people of Makkah may return to your religion, which is the religion of Abraham."

It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended order is: "Indeed He will guide me, so that they may return, and He made it..." etc. Al-Suddi said: "so that they may repent, and thus return from what they are upon to the worship of Allah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned His favour upon Quraysh and those disbelievers of their time who agreed with them, so He said: ﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and to their fathers﴾. He turned away from the first speech to mention what He gave them enjoyment of, in souls, families, wealth, and kinds of blessings, and what He gave enjoyment of to their fathers, and He did not hasten punishment upon them. So they were deceived by the respite and devoted themselves to desires, ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning of mubin ("clear") is: manifest and clear in its message, or: one who makes clear to them what they need of the matters of religion. But they did not respond to him, nor did they act upon what was sent down to him.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear what they did when the truth came, so He said: ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."﴾ That is: deniers. So they called the Qur'an magic and denied it, and they belittled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?"﴾ By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if. By the two men is meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if, as Qatadah and others said. Mujahid and others said: ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah from Makkah and ʿUmayr ibn ʿAbd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. It has also been said otherwise.

The apparent sense of the wording is that the intended meaning is a man from one of the two towns, great in standing, wide in wealth, and a leader among his people. The meaning is: if it were a Qur'an, it would have been sent down upon a great man among the great ones of the two towns.

Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ meaning prophethood, or what is more general than it. The interrogative is for denial.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 2 of 2):

Then He (glorified is He) explained that it is He who apportioned among them the means of their livelihood in worldly affairs, so He said: ﴿It is We who apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾. He did not delegate that to them, and no one among the servants has the right to exercise authority over anything. Rather, judgement belongs to Allah alone. Since Allah (glorified is He) is the One who apportioned their provisions among them and raised some of them above others in rank, how then should they not be content with His apportioning in the matter of prophethood and His entrusting it to whomever He wills of His creation?

Muqatil said: He means, "Do they hold the keys of the Message, so that they place it wherever they wish?"

The majority of readers recited مَعِيشَتَهم (ma'ishatahum, "their livelihood") in the singular, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin recited مَعايِشَهم (ma'ayishahum, "their livelihoods") in the plural. The meaning of ﴿And We raised some of them above others in ranks﴾ is that He made distinctions among them, so that some were more excellent than others in worldly matters: in provision, leadership, strength, freedom, intellect and knowledge. Then He mentioned the reason for raising some of them in rank above others, saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾. That is, so that some may employ others: the wealthy employs the poor, the leader employs the subordinate, the strong employs the weak, the free employs the slave, the one of greater intellect employs the one below him in intellect, and the learned employs the ignorant. This holds in most circumstances of the people of this world, and by it their interests are fulfilled, their livelihood is organised, and each one of them attains what he seeks. For every worldly craft is practised well by one group and not by others, so some were made in need of others, so that consolation may be achieved among them in the enjoyment of worldly goods. This one needs that one, this one makes for that one, and this one gives to that one.

As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "We subjected" means "We gave them servants and attendants, so that the rich employ the poor, and thus some of them become a means of livelihood for others." Qatadah and ad-Dahhak said: "so that some may possess others." It has also been said that السُّخْرِيّ (sukhriyy) here is the sense of "mockery" (istihza'). Although this matches the lexical meaning, it is far from the meaning of the Qur'an and contrary to the intended context.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾. By "mercy" is meant what Allah has prepared for His righteous servants in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is prophethood, since it is what is meant by "mercy" in the earlier words: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾. There is no barrier to meaning by it everything that is called "mercy", either by inclusion or by substitution (badal). The phrase مِمّا يَجْمَعُونَ (mimma yajma'un, "than what they accumulate") means: what they accumulate of wealth and all the other goods of this world.

Then He (glorified is He) explained the insignificance of this world in His sight, so He said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾, that is, were it not that they would all gather in disbelief out of inclination toward this world and its adornment, ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver ceilings for their houses﴾. He used the plural pronoun in لِبُيُوتِهِمْ (libuyutihim, "for their houses") and the singular in يَكْفُرُ (yakfuru, "disbelieves") with regard to the meaning and the wording of مَن (man, "whoever"). لِبُيُوتِهِمْ is a بَدَل اشْتِمال (badal ishtimal, a substitution of inclusion) from the relative pronoun. السُّقُفُ (suqufun, "ceilings") is the plural of سَقْفٌ (saqf, "ceiling").

The majority recited سُقُفًا with a ḍammah on the sīn and the qāf, like رَهْنٌ and رُهُنٌ. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "There is no third form like them." Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of سَقِيفٌ (saqif), like كَثِيبٌ and كُثُبٌ, and رَغِيفٌ and رُغُفٌ. It has also been said that it is the plural of سُقُوفٌ (suquf), so it is a plural of a plural. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited سَقْفًا with a fatḥah on the sīn and a sukūn on the qāf, in the singular, and its meaning is plural because it is a generic noun (li-l-jins).

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is: were it not that people would all disbelieve because of their inclination toward this world and their leaving the Hereafter, We would have given them in this world what We have described, because of the insignificance of this world in the sight of Allah. Most of the exegetes held this view.

Ibn Zayd said: "Were it not that mankind would become one community" means, in the pursuit of this world and their preference for it over the Hereafter.

Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is: were it not that among the disbelievers there were rich and poor, and among the Muslims there were the same, We would have given the disbelievers of this world all of this, because of its insignificance. ﴿And staircases on which they ascend﴾. (p-1340) The مَعارِج (ma'arij) are the stairs, the plural of مِعراج (mi'raj), and the mi'raj is the ladder.

Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may make the singular مِعْرَجًا (mi'rajan) and مَعْرَجًا (ma'rajan), like مِرْقاةٌ and مَرْقاةٌ. The meaning is: We would have made for them staircases of silver, upon which they ascend, that is, they climb and ascend by means of the staircases. It is said: ظَهَرْتُ عَلى البَيْتِ (zahartu 'ala al-bayt, "I ascended onto the house"), meaning I rose to its roof. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"We reached the heavens in glory, honour and lordship, and indeed we hope for a higher ascent beyond that."

That is, a place to ascend.

﴿And doors for their houses, and couches on which they recline﴾. That is, We would have made for their houses doors of silver and couches of silver, ﴿on which they recline﴾. That is, on the couches, which is the plural of سَرِيرٌ (sarir). It has also been said it is the plural of أَسِرَّةٌ (asirrah), so it is a plural of a plural. الِاتِّكاء (al-ittika') and التَّوَكُّؤ (tawakkus) mean leaning heavily upon something, as in ﴿I lean upon it﴾ [Taha: 18], and one says اتَّكَأ عَلى الشَّيْءِ (ittaka'a 'ala al-shay'), so he is مُتَّكِئٌ (muttaki'), and the place is مُتَّكَأٌ (muttaka'). The زُخْرُف (zukhruf) is gold. It has also been said that it is adornment in general, whether gold or otherwise. Ibn Zayd said: it is what people make for their homes of furnishings and household goods. Al-Hasan said: it is decorative designs, and its root meaning is adornment; one says زَخْرَفْتُ الدّارَ (zakhraftu al-dar, "I adorned the house"), meaning I decorated it.

The accusative of زُخْرُفًا (zukhrufan) is either by a verb understood, meaning: "and We would have made for them, in addition to all that, adornment", or by removal of the preposition, meaning: "doors and couches of silver and of gold", and when the preposition is removed, the noun becomes accusative.

Then He (glorified is He) informed that all of that is only enjoyed in this world, so He said: ﴿And all that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. The majority recited لَمّا (lamma) with a light pronunciation, while 'Asim, Hamzah and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited it with the doubled mīm (lammā). On the first reading, إنْ (in) is the light form of the heavy إنَّ, and on the second reading it is a negation, and لَمّا has the sense of إلّا (illa, "except"), meaning: "all that is nothing but a thing enjoyed in this world."

Abu Raja' recited لِمّا with a kasrah on the lām, on the basis that the lām indicates cause and مّا is a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted: that is, for that which is an enjoyment.

﴿But the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾. That is, for whoever guards against polytheism and sins, believes in Allah alone and acts in obedience to Him, for it is the enduring one that does not perish, and its everlasting bounty does not cease.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿We found our fathers upon a community﴾: "upon a religion."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him concerning ﴿And He made it a word that remains﴾: "There is no god but Allah" in his posterity, and he said: "The posterity of Ibrahim, his son."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him, that he was asked about the saying of Allah ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾ "What are the two towns?" He said: "al-Ta'if and Makkah." It was said: "Who are the two men?" He said: "'Umayr ibn Mas'ud, and the best of the Quraysh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him: "By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if, and the great one is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Qurashi and Habib ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning the verse: "They mean: more honourable than Muhammad, [namely] al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from the people of Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from the people of al-Ta'if."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning His saying ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾ and the rest of the verse: "He says: Were it not that We would make all mankind disbelievers, We would have made for the houses of the disbelievers ceilings of silver, and staircases of silver, which are steps upon which they ascend to the upper rooms, and couches of silver, and zukhruf, which is gold."

At-Tirmidhi related it and authenticated it, and Ibn Majah related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single drink of water from it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ Am (أمْ) here is the disjunctive (al-munqati'a) "am," meaning "rather": "Did We give them a Book before the Qur'an, by which they worship other than Allah?" ﴿So they hold fast to it﴾ means they take up what is in it, argue by it, and make it a proof for themselves. It is also possible that am is a repetition of His saying "Did they witness their creation?", in which case it is connected (muttasila), and the meaning is: "Were they present at their creation, or have We given them a Book...?"

It has been said that the pronoun in min qablihi ("before this") refers to their claim, meaning: "Or have We given them a Book before their claim, which testifies to the soundness of what they claim?" The first view is preferable.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that they have no proof in their hands and no basis for doubt, but that they followed their fathers in misguidance. So He said: ﴿Nay, they say: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community (ummah), and indeed we are guided in their footsteps."﴾ Thus they acknowledged that they have no foundation except the blind imitation (taqlid) of their fathers. The meaning of ʿalā ummatin ("upon a community") is "upon a path and a creed." Abu ʿUbayd said: it is the path and the religion, and Qatadah and others said the same. Al-Jawhari said: the ummah is the path and the religion. It is said: "So-and-so has no ummah," meaning he has no religion and no sect. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"We were upon the ummah of our fathers, and we follow the first ones, the first ones."

And the saying of another:

"Is one who has an ummah equal to one who is ungrateful?"

Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: "upon a qiblah (direction of prayer)." Al-Akhfash said: "upon uprightness," and he recited the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I swore and I left no doubt for you, and does one who has an ummah sin while he is obedient?"

The majority read ummatin with a damma on the hamza (أُمَّةٍ). Mujahid, Qatadah, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz read it with a kasra (إِمَّةٍ).

Al-Jawhari said: al-immah (إِمَّة) with a kasra means "blessing," and al-immah is also a dialectal variant of al-ummah. From this is the saying of ʿAdi ibn Zayd:

"Then after prosperity and kingship and the ummah (al-umm-ah), the graves have buried them there."

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that others among the disbelievers before them had already reached this same statement and held it: ﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ Mutrafuha ("its affluent ones") means its wealthy and its leaders. Qatadah said: muqtadun means "following." The meanings of being guided (ihtida') and following (iqtida') are close, and He specified "the affluent" to draw attention to the fact that luxury is the cause of neglecting reflection.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them, so He said: ﴿He said: "Even if I brought you something better guiding than what you found your fathers upon?"﴾ That is: "Will you follow your fathers even if I bring you a religion better guided than the religion of your fathers?" Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Say to them: Will you follow what you found your fathers upon, even if I bring you something better than it?"

The majority read qul awa-law ji'tukum ("Say: even if I brought you"). Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read qala awa-law ji'tukum ("He said"). This is a narration of what took place between the warners and their peoples: each warner from those warners said to his community. It has also been said that both readings narrate what took place between the prophets and their peoples, as if it were said to each prophet: "Say," on the evidence of His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾

This is among the greatest proofs demonstrating the invalidity and ugliness of taqlid. These blind followers in Islam only act on the sayings of their predecessors, follow their traces, and imitate them. So when the one calling to the truth wishes to bring them out of misguidance or to repel them from an innovation which they have held fast to and inherited from their predecessors, without a clear proof or an evident argument, but merely by saying and what is said, with a false doubt, a worthless argument, and a baseless statement, they respond with what the affluent of these creeds said: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps,﴾ or with something whose meaning is close to that. If the one calling to the truth says to them: "The Islamic community has united us, and this Muhammadan religion has encompassed us, and Allah has not required us, nor you, nor your fathers before you, to worship except by His Book which He sent down to His Messenger, and by what is authentically related from His Messenger, for he is the one who makes clear the Book of Allah, clarifies its meanings, and distinguishes between its clear (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih) verses. So let us come and refer what we dispute to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, as Allah commanded us in His Book by His saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], for referring to them both is better guidance for us and for you than referring to what your predecessors said and what your fathers followed," they recoil like wild beasts and pelt the one calling them with every stone and clod, as if they had never heard the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ [al-Nur: 51], nor His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then they find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided, and they submit with full submission.﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]

If the one speaking says to them: "This scholar whom you imitate and whose sayings you follow is like you in that he is obligated to follow the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and is required to do what you are required to do. And when he acts by his own opinion because he does not find the evidence, that is a concession (rukhsah) for him, which it is not permissible for another to follow him in, nor lawful for him to act upon. Here I am, producing for you the evidence which he did not find, from the Book of Allah or from what is authentically established of the Sunnah of His Messenger, and that is better for you than what you found your fathers upon," they say: "We will not act on this, and there is no hearing and no obedience for you." They find in their hearts the greatest discomfort with the judgment of the Book and the Sunnah, and do not submit to it or accept it. Satan has given them a staff to lean on whenever they hear someone calling them to the Book and the Sunnah, which is that they say: "Our imam whom we imitated and followed knows the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger better than you do." This is because their minds have formed a great image of those whom they follow, due to the antiquity of the era and the multitude of followers. They do not realize that this claim is turned against them and repelled back into their faces. For if it were said to them: "There are among the Successors (tabi'un) those who are greater in rank and earlier in era than your companion. If antiquity of era and nobility of rank had a merit that necessitates following, then come, and I will show you one who is earlier in era and greater in rank." If they refuse that, then here I am, guiding you to one who is greater in rank, more eminent in standing, more numerous in followers, and earlier in era: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, our Prophet and your Prophet, the Messenger of Allah to us and to you. So come, for his Sunnah is present in the records and registers of Islam, which the whole of this community has received, generation after generation and era after era. And this is the Book of our Lord, the Creator of all, the Provider of all, and the Originator of all, present among us, found in every house and in the hand of every Muslim, which has not been altered, changed, added to, diminished, distorted, or corrupted. We and you are among those who understand its words and grasp its meanings. So come, let us take the truth from its source and drink the pure water from its spring, for it is better guided than what you found your fathers upon." They say: "No hearing and no obedience," either by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of state. So reflect on this and consider it, if any remnant of fairness remains in you, a portion of goodness, a shred of modesty, and a share of religion. There is no power and no strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

I have explained this in the utmost clarity in my book which I named Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab. Refer to it if you wish that the darkness of partisanship be lifted from you and the clouds of taqlid be dispersed for you.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ — and that vengeance is what Allah inflicted upon the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud. ﴿So look how was the end of the deniers﴾ from those nations, for their traces are still present.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾ — that is: mention to them the time when he said to his father and his people, who imitated their fathers and worshipped idols: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. Al-Bara' ("free") is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective for emphasis, and it is used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine, and the feminine. Al-Jawhari said: "I disassociated myself from such-and-such, and I am free of it (bara' wa khala')," and it is not made dual or plural, because it is originally a masdar.

Then He excepted his Creator from the disassociation, so He said: ﴿Except He who originated me﴾, meaning: who created me, ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾, meaning: He will direct me to His religion and keep me firm upon the truth. The exception is either disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but He who originated me," or connected (muttasil), from the generality of ma ("what"), since they used to worship Allah and the idols together. His statement that He will certainly guide him reflects his firm trust in Allah, glorified is He, and the strength of his certainty.

﴿And He made it a word that remains in his posterity﴾. The pronoun in ja'alaha ("made it") refers to His saying: ﴿except He who originated me﴾, and it means monotheism, as if he said: "And He made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham, who are his descendants, so there will always be among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah, glorified is He." The subject of ja'alaha is Abraham, since he enjoined monotheism upon them and commanded them to adhere to it, as in His saying: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and so on. It has been said that the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, meaning: Allah, mighty and majestic is He, made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham. The ʿaqib ("posterity") means those who come after.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: the word is "There is no god but Allah," and there will always be from his posterity someone who worships Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Ikrimah said: it is Islam. Ibn Zayd said: the word is His saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. The clause ﴿so that they may return﴾ is a justification for the making (ja'l), meaning: He made it remain in hope that whoever among them associates partners with Allah would return to it by calling upon the One who affirms His oneness.

It has also been said that the pronoun in la'allahum ("so that they") refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: "so that the people of Makkah may return to your religion, which is the religion of Abraham."

It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended order is: "Indeed He will guide me, so that they may return, and He made it..." etc. Al-Suddi said: "so that they may repent, and thus return from what they are upon to the worship of Allah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned His favour upon Quraysh and those disbelievers of their time who agreed with them, so He said: ﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and to their fathers﴾. He turned away from the first speech to mention what He gave them enjoyment of, in souls, families, wealth, and kinds of blessings, and what He gave enjoyment of to their fathers, and He did not hasten punishment upon them. So they were deceived by the respite and devoted themselves to desires, ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning of mubin ("clear") is: manifest and clear in its message, or: one who makes clear to them what they need of the matters of religion. But they did not respond to him, nor did they act upon what was sent down to him.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear what they did when the truth came, so He said: ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."﴾ That is: deniers. So they called the Qur'an magic and denied it, and they belittled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?"﴾ By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if. By the two men is meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if, as Qatadah and others said. Mujahid and others said: ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah from Makkah and ʿUmayr ibn ʿAbd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. It has also been said otherwise.

The apparent sense of the wording is that the intended meaning is a man from one of the two towns, great in standing, wide in wealth, and a leader among his people. The meaning is: if it were a Qur'an, it would have been sent down upon a great man among the great ones of the two towns.

Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ meaning prophethood, or what is more general than it. The interrogative is for denial.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 2 of 2):

Then He (glorified is He) explained that it is He who apportioned among them the means of their livelihood in worldly affairs, so He said: ﴿It is We who apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾. He did not delegate that to them, and no one among the servants has the right to exercise authority over anything. Rather, judgement belongs to Allah alone. Since Allah (glorified is He) is the One who apportioned their provisions among them and raised some of them above others in rank, how then should they not be content with His apportioning in the matter of prophethood and His entrusting it to whomever He wills of His creation?

Muqatil said: He means, "Do they hold the keys of the Message, so that they place it wherever they wish?"

The majority of readers recited مَعِيشَتَهم (ma'ishatahum, "their livelihood") in the singular, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin recited مَعايِشَهم (ma'ayishahum, "their livelihoods") in the plural. The meaning of ﴿And We raised some of them above others in ranks﴾ is that He made distinctions among them, so that some were more excellent than others in worldly matters: in provision, leadership, strength, freedom, intellect and knowledge. Then He mentioned the reason for raising some of them in rank above others, saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾. That is, so that some may employ others: the wealthy employs the poor, the leader employs the subordinate, the strong employs the weak, the free employs the slave, the one of greater intellect employs the one below him in intellect, and the learned employs the ignorant. This holds in most circumstances of the people of this world, and by it their interests are fulfilled, their livelihood is organised, and each one of them attains what he seeks. For every worldly craft is practised well by one group and not by others, so some were made in need of others, so that consolation may be achieved among them in the enjoyment of worldly goods. This one needs that one, this one makes for that one, and this one gives to that one.

As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "We subjected" means "We gave them servants and attendants, so that the rich employ the poor, and thus some of them become a means of livelihood for others." Qatadah and ad-Dahhak said: "so that some may possess others." It has also been said that السُّخْرِيّ (sukhriyy) here is the sense of "mockery" (istihza'). Although this matches the lexical meaning, it is far from the meaning of the Qur'an and contrary to the intended context.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾. By "mercy" is meant what Allah has prepared for His righteous servants in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is prophethood, since it is what is meant by "mercy" in the earlier words: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾. There is no barrier to meaning by it everything that is called "mercy", either by inclusion or by substitution (badal). The phrase مِمّا يَجْمَعُونَ (mimma yajma'un, "than what they accumulate") means: what they accumulate of wealth and all the other goods of this world.

Then He (glorified is He) explained the insignificance of this world in His sight, so He said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾, that is, were it not that they would all gather in disbelief out of inclination toward this world and its adornment, ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver ceilings for their houses﴾. He used the plural pronoun in لِبُيُوتِهِمْ (libuyutihim, "for their houses") and the singular in يَكْفُرُ (yakfuru, "disbelieves") with regard to the meaning and the wording of مَن (man, "whoever"). لِبُيُوتِهِمْ is a بَدَل اشْتِمال (badal ishtimal, a substitution of inclusion) from the relative pronoun. السُّقُفُ (suqufun, "ceilings") is the plural of سَقْفٌ (saqf, "ceiling").

The majority recited سُقُفًا with a ḍammah on the sīn and the qāf, like رَهْنٌ and رُهُنٌ. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "There is no third form like them." Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of سَقِيفٌ (saqif), like كَثِيبٌ and كُثُبٌ, and رَغِيفٌ and رُغُفٌ. It has also been said that it is the plural of سُقُوفٌ (suquf), so it is a plural of a plural. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited سَقْفًا with a fatḥah on the sīn and a sukūn on the qāf, in the singular, and its meaning is plural because it is a generic noun (li-l-jins).

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is: were it not that people would all disbelieve because of their inclination toward this world and their leaving the Hereafter, We would have given them in this world what We have described, because of the insignificance of this world in the sight of Allah. Most of the exegetes held this view.

Ibn Zayd said: "Were it not that mankind would become one community" means, in the pursuit of this world and their preference for it over the Hereafter.

Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is: were it not that among the disbelievers there were rich and poor, and among the Muslims there were the same, We would have given the disbelievers of this world all of this, because of its insignificance. ﴿And staircases on which they ascend﴾. (p-1340) The مَعارِج (ma'arij) are the stairs, the plural of مِعراج (mi'raj), and the mi'raj is the ladder.

Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may make the singular مِعْرَجًا (mi'rajan) and مَعْرَجًا (ma'rajan), like مِرْقاةٌ and مَرْقاةٌ. The meaning is: We would have made for them staircases of silver, upon which they ascend, that is, they climb and ascend by means of the staircases. It is said: ظَهَرْتُ عَلى البَيْتِ (zahartu 'ala al-bayt, "I ascended onto the house"), meaning I rose to its roof. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"We reached the heavens in glory, honour and lordship, and indeed we hope for a higher ascent beyond that."

That is, a place to ascend.

﴿And doors for their houses, and couches on which they recline﴾. That is, We would have made for their houses doors of silver and couches of silver, ﴿on which they recline﴾. That is, on the couches, which is the plural of سَرِيرٌ (sarir). It has also been said it is the plural of أَسِرَّةٌ (asirrah), so it is a plural of a plural. الِاتِّكاء (al-ittika') and التَّوَكُّؤ (tawakkus) mean leaning heavily upon something, as in ﴿I lean upon it﴾ [Taha: 18], and one says اتَّكَأ عَلى الشَّيْءِ (ittaka'a 'ala al-shay'), so he is مُتَّكِئٌ (muttaki'), and the place is مُتَّكَأٌ (muttaka'). The زُخْرُف (zukhruf) is gold. It has also been said that it is adornment in general, whether gold or otherwise. Ibn Zayd said: it is what people make for their homes of furnishings and household goods. Al-Hasan said: it is decorative designs, and its root meaning is adornment; one says زَخْرَفْتُ الدّارَ (zakhraftu al-dar, "I adorned the house"), meaning I decorated it.

The accusative of زُخْرُفًا (zukhrufan) is either by a verb understood, meaning: "and We would have made for them, in addition to all that, adornment", or by removal of the preposition, meaning: "doors and couches of silver and of gold", and when the preposition is removed, the noun becomes accusative.

Then He (glorified is He) informed that all of that is only enjoyed in this world, so He said: ﴿And all that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. The majority recited لَمّا (lamma) with a light pronunciation, while 'Asim, Hamzah and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited it with the doubled mīm (lammā). On the first reading, إنْ (in) is the light form of the heavy إنَّ, and on the second reading it is a negation, and لَمّا has the sense of إلّا (illa, "except"), meaning: "all that is nothing but a thing enjoyed in this world."

Abu Raja' recited لِمّا with a kasrah on the lām, on the basis that the lām indicates cause and مّا is a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted: that is, for that which is an enjoyment.

﴿But the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾. That is, for whoever guards against polytheism and sins, believes in Allah alone and acts in obedience to Him, for it is the enduring one that does not perish, and its everlasting bounty does not cease.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿We found our fathers upon a community﴾: "upon a religion."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him concerning ﴿And He made it a word that remains﴾: "There is no god but Allah" in his posterity, and he said: "The posterity of Ibrahim, his son."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him, that he was asked about the saying of Allah ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾ "What are the two towns?" He said: "al-Ta'if and Makkah." It was said: "Who are the two men?" He said: "'Umayr ibn Mas'ud, and the best of the Quraysh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him: "By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if, and the great one is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Qurashi and Habib ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning the verse: "They mean: more honourable than Muhammad, [namely] al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from the people of Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from the people of al-Ta'if."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning His saying ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾ and the rest of the verse: "He says: Were it not that We would make all mankind disbelievers, We would have made for the houses of the disbelievers ceilings of silver, and staircases of silver, which are steps upon which they ascend to the upper rooms, and couches of silver, and zukhruf, which is gold."

At-Tirmidhi related it and authenticated it, and Ibn Majah related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single drink of water from it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ Am (أمْ) here is the disjunctive (al-munqati'a) "am," meaning "rather": "Did We give them a Book before the Qur'an, by which they worship other than Allah?" ﴿So they hold fast to it﴾ means they take up what is in it, argue by it, and make it a proof for themselves. It is also possible that am is a repetition of His saying "Did they witness their creation?", in which case it is connected (muttasila), and the meaning is: "Were they present at their creation, or have We given them a Book...?"

It has been said that the pronoun in min qablihi ("before this") refers to their claim, meaning: "Or have We given them a Book before their claim, which testifies to the soundness of what they claim?" The first view is preferable.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that they have no proof in their hands and no basis for doubt, but that they followed their fathers in misguidance. So He said: ﴿Nay, they say: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community (ummah), and indeed we are guided in their footsteps."﴾ Thus they acknowledged that they have no foundation except the blind imitation (taqlid) of their fathers. The meaning of ʿalā ummatin ("upon a community") is "upon a path and a creed." Abu ʿUbayd said: it is the path and the religion, and Qatadah and others said the same. Al-Jawhari said: the ummah is the path and the religion. It is said: "So-and-so has no ummah," meaning he has no religion and no sect. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"We were upon the ummah of our fathers, and we follow the first ones, the first ones."

And the saying of another:

"Is one who has an ummah equal to one who is ungrateful?"

Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: "upon a qiblah (direction of prayer)." Al-Akhfash said: "upon uprightness," and he recited the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I swore and I left no doubt for you, and does one who has an ummah sin while he is obedient?"

The majority read ummatin with a damma on the hamza (أُمَّةٍ). Mujahid, Qatadah, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz read it with a kasra (إِمَّةٍ).

Al-Jawhari said: al-immah (إِمَّة) with a kasra means "blessing," and al-immah is also a dialectal variant of al-ummah. From this is the saying of ʿAdi ibn Zayd:

"Then after prosperity and kingship and the ummah (al-umm-ah), the graves have buried them there."

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that others among the disbelievers before them had already reached this same statement and held it: ﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ Mutrafuha ("its affluent ones") means its wealthy and its leaders. Qatadah said: muqtadun means "following." The meanings of being guided (ihtida') and following (iqtida') are close, and He specified "the affluent" to draw attention to the fact that luxury is the cause of neglecting reflection.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them, so He said: ﴿He said: "Even if I brought you something better guiding than what you found your fathers upon?"﴾ That is: "Will you follow your fathers even if I bring you a religion better guided than the religion of your fathers?" Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Say to them: Will you follow what you found your fathers upon, even if I bring you something better than it?"

The majority read qul awa-law ji'tukum ("Say: even if I brought you"). Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read qala awa-law ji'tukum ("He said"). This is a narration of what took place between the warners and their peoples: each warner from those warners said to his community. It has also been said that both readings narrate what took place between the prophets and their peoples, as if it were said to each prophet: "Say," on the evidence of His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾

This is among the greatest proofs demonstrating the invalidity and ugliness of taqlid. These blind followers in Islam only act on the sayings of their predecessors, follow their traces, and imitate them. So when the one calling to the truth wishes to bring them out of misguidance or to repel them from an innovation which they have held fast to and inherited from their predecessors, without a clear proof or an evident argument, but merely by saying and what is said, with a false doubt, a worthless argument, and a baseless statement, they respond with what the affluent of these creeds said: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps,﴾ or with something whose meaning is close to that. If the one calling to the truth says to them: "The Islamic community has united us, and this Muhammadan religion has encompassed us, and Allah has not required us, nor you, nor your fathers before you, to worship except by His Book which He sent down to His Messenger, and by what is authentically related from His Messenger, for he is the one who makes clear the Book of Allah, clarifies its meanings, and distinguishes between its clear (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih) verses. So let us come and refer what we dispute to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, as Allah commanded us in His Book by His saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], for referring to them both is better guidance for us and for you than referring to what your predecessors said and what your fathers followed," they recoil like wild beasts and pelt the one calling them with every stone and clod, as if they had never heard the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ [al-Nur: 51], nor His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then they find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided, and they submit with full submission.﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]

If the one speaking says to them: "This scholar whom you imitate and whose sayings you follow is like you in that he is obligated to follow the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and is required to do what you are required to do. And when he acts by his own opinion because he does not find the evidence, that is a concession (rukhsah) for him, which it is not permissible for another to follow him in, nor lawful for him to act upon. Here I am, producing for you the evidence which he did not find, from the Book of Allah or from what is authentically established of the Sunnah of His Messenger, and that is better for you than what you found your fathers upon," they say: "We will not act on this, and there is no hearing and no obedience for you." They find in their hearts the greatest discomfort with the judgment of the Book and the Sunnah, and do not submit to it or accept it. Satan has given them a staff to lean on whenever they hear someone calling them to the Book and the Sunnah, which is that they say: "Our imam whom we imitated and followed knows the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger better than you do." This is because their minds have formed a great image of those whom they follow, due to the antiquity of the era and the multitude of followers. They do not realize that this claim is turned against them and repelled back into their faces. For if it were said to them: "There are among the Successors (tabi'un) those who are greater in rank and earlier in era than your companion. If antiquity of era and nobility of rank had a merit that necessitates following, then come, and I will show you one who is earlier in era and greater in rank." If they refuse that, then here I am, guiding you to one who is greater in rank, more eminent in standing, more numerous in followers, and earlier in era: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, our Prophet and your Prophet, the Messenger of Allah to us and to you. So come, for his Sunnah is present in the records and registers of Islam, which the whole of this community has received, generation after generation and era after era. And this is the Book of our Lord, the Creator of all, the Provider of all, and the Originator of all, present among us, found in every house and in the hand of every Muslim, which has not been altered, changed, added to, diminished, distorted, or corrupted. We and you are among those who understand its words and grasp its meanings. So come, let us take the truth from its source and drink the pure water from its spring, for it is better guided than what you found your fathers upon." They say: "No hearing and no obedience," either by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of state. So reflect on this and consider it, if any remnant of fairness remains in you, a portion of goodness, a shred of modesty, and a share of religion. There is no power and no strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

I have explained this in the utmost clarity in my book which I named Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab. Refer to it if you wish that the darkness of partisanship be lifted from you and the clouds of taqlid be dispersed for you.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ — and that vengeance is what Allah inflicted upon the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud. ﴿So look how was the end of the deniers﴾ from those nations, for their traces are still present.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾ — that is: mention to them the time when he said to his father and his people, who imitated their fathers and worshipped idols: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. Al-Bara' ("free") is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective for emphasis, and it is used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine, and the feminine. Al-Jawhari said: "I disassociated myself from such-and-such, and I am free of it (bara' wa khala')," and it is not made dual or plural, because it is originally a masdar.

Then He excepted his Creator from the disassociation, so He said: ﴿Except He who originated me﴾, meaning: who created me, ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾, meaning: He will direct me to His religion and keep me firm upon the truth. The exception is either disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but He who originated me," or connected (muttasil), from the generality of ma ("what"), since they used to worship Allah and the idols together. His statement that He will certainly guide him reflects his firm trust in Allah, glorified is He, and the strength of his certainty.

﴿And He made it a word that remains in his posterity﴾. The pronoun in ja'alaha ("made it") refers to His saying: ﴿except He who originated me﴾, and it means monotheism, as if he said: "And He made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham, who are his descendants, so there will always be among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah, glorified is He." The subject of ja'alaha is Abraham, since he enjoined monotheism upon them and commanded them to adhere to it, as in His saying: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and so on. It has been said that the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, meaning: Allah, mighty and majestic is He, made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham. The ʿaqib ("posterity") means those who come after.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: the word is "There is no god but Allah," and there will always be from his posterity someone who worships Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Ikrimah said: it is Islam. Ibn Zayd said: the word is His saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. The clause ﴿so that they may return﴾ is a justification for the making (ja'l), meaning: He made it remain in hope that whoever among them associates partners with Allah would return to it by calling upon the One who affirms His oneness.

It has also been said that the pronoun in la'allahum ("so that they") refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: "so that the people of Makkah may return to your religion, which is the religion of Abraham."

It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended order is: "Indeed He will guide me, so that they may return, and He made it..." etc. Al-Suddi said: "so that they may repent, and thus return from what they are upon to the worship of Allah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned His favour upon Quraysh and those disbelievers of their time who agreed with them, so He said: ﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and to their fathers﴾. He turned away from the first speech to mention what He gave them enjoyment of, in souls, families, wealth, and kinds of blessings, and what He gave enjoyment of to their fathers, and He did not hasten punishment upon them. So they were deceived by the respite and devoted themselves to desires, ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning of mubin ("clear") is: manifest and clear in its message, or: one who makes clear to them what they need of the matters of religion. But they did not respond to him, nor did they act upon what was sent down to him.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear what they did when the truth came, so He said: ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."﴾ That is: deniers. So they called the Qur'an magic and denied it, and they belittled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?"﴾ By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if. By the two men is meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if, as Qatadah and others said. Mujahid and others said: ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah from Makkah and ʿUmayr ibn ʿAbd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. It has also been said otherwise.

The apparent sense of the wording is that the intended meaning is a man from one of the two towns, great in standing, wide in wealth, and a leader among his people. The meaning is: if it were a Qur'an, it would have been sent down upon a great man among the great ones of the two towns.

Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ meaning prophethood, or what is more general than it. The interrogative is for denial.
