So come, let us take the truth from its source and drink the pure water from its spring, for it is better guided than what you found your fathers upon." They say: "No hearing and no obedience," either by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of state. So reflect on this and consider it, if any remnant of fairness remains in you, a portion of goodness, a shred of modesty, and a share of religion. There is no power and no strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

I have explained this in the utmost clarity in my book which I named Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab. Refer to it if you wish that the darkness of partisanship be lifted from you and the clouds of taqlid be dispersed for you.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ — and that vengeance is what Allah inflicted upon the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud. ﴿So look how was the end of the deniers﴾ from those nations, for their traces are still present.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾ — that is: mention to them the time when he said to his father and his people, who imitated their fathers and worshipped idols: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. Al-Bara' ("free") is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective for emphasis, and it is used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine, and the feminine. Al-Jawhari said: "I disassociated myself from such-and-such, and I am free of it (bara' wa khala')," and it is not made dual or plural, because it is originally a masdar.

Then He excepted his Creator from the disassociation, so He said: ﴿Except He who originated me﴾, meaning: who created me, ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾, meaning: He will direct me to His religion and keep me firm upon the truth. The exception is either disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but He who originated me," or connected (muttasil), from the generality of ma ("what"), since they used to worship Allah and the idols together. His statement that He will certainly guide him reflects his firm trust in Allah, glorified is He, and the strength of his certainty.

﴿And He made it a word that remains in his posterity﴾. The pronoun in ja'alaha ("made it") refers to His saying: ﴿except He who originated me﴾, and it means monotheism, as if he said: "And He made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham, who are his descendants, so there will always be among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah, glorified is He." The subject of ja'alaha is Abraham, since he enjoined monotheism upon them and commanded them to adhere to it, as in His saying: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and so on. It has been said that the subject is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, meaning: Allah, mighty and majestic is He, made the word of monotheism remain in the posterity of Abraham. The ʿaqib ("posterity") means those who come after.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: the word is "There is no god but Allah," and there will always be from his posterity someone who worships Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Ikrimah said: it is Islam. Ibn Zayd said: the word is His saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. The clause ﴿so that they may return﴾ is a justification for the making (ja'l), meaning: He made it remain in hope that whoever among them associates partners with Allah would return to it by calling upon the One who affirms His oneness.

It has also been said that the pronoun in la'allahum ("so that they") refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: "so that the people of Makkah may return to your religion, which is the religion of Abraham."

It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended order is: "Indeed He will guide me, so that they may return, and He made it..." etc. Al-Suddi said: "so that they may repent, and thus return from what they are upon to the worship of Allah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned His favour upon Quraysh and those disbelievers of their time who agreed with them, so He said: ﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and to their fathers﴾. He turned away from the first speech to mention what He gave them enjoyment of, in souls, families, wealth, and kinds of blessings, and what He gave enjoyment of to their fathers, and He did not hasten punishment upon them. So they were deceived by the respite and devoted themselves to desires, ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning of mubin ("clear") is: manifest and clear in its message, or: one who makes clear to them what they need of the matters of religion. But they did not respond to him, nor did they act upon what was sent down to him.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear what they did when the truth came, so He said: ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."﴾ That is: deniers. So they called the Qur'an magic and denied it, and they belittled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?"﴾ By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if. By the two men is meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if, as Qatadah and others said. Mujahid and others said: ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah from Makkah and ʿUmayr ibn ʿAbd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. It has also been said otherwise.

The apparent sense of the wording is that the intended meaning is a man from one of the two towns, great in standing, wide in wealth, and a leader among his people. The meaning is: if it were a Qur'an, it would have been sent down upon a great man among the great ones of the two towns.

Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ meaning prophethood, or what is more general than it. The interrogative is for denial.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 21–35 (part 2 of 2):

Then He (glorified is He) explained that it is He who apportioned among them the means of their livelihood in worldly affairs, so He said: ﴿It is We who apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾. He did not delegate that to them, and no one among the servants has the right to exercise authority over anything. Rather, judgement belongs to Allah alone. Since Allah (glorified is He) is the One who apportioned their provisions among them and raised some of them above others in rank, how then should they not be content with His apportioning in the matter of prophethood and His entrusting it to whomever He wills of His creation?

Muqatil said: He means, "Do they hold the keys of the Message, so that they place it wherever they wish?"

The majority of readers recited مَعِيشَتَهم (ma'ishatahum, "their livelihood") in the singular, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin recited مَعايِشَهم (ma'ayishahum, "their livelihoods") in the plural. The meaning of ﴿And We raised some of them above others in ranks﴾ is that He made distinctions among them, so that some were more excellent than others in worldly matters: in provision, leadership, strength, freedom, intellect and knowledge. Then He mentioned the reason for raising some of them in rank above others, saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾. That is, so that some may employ others: the wealthy employs the poor, the leader employs the subordinate, the strong employs the weak, the free employs the slave, the one of greater intellect employs the one below him in intellect, and the learned employs the ignorant. This holds in most circumstances of the people of this world, and by it their interests are fulfilled, their livelihood is organised, and each one of them attains what he seeks. For every worldly craft is practised well by one group and not by others, so some were made in need of others, so that consolation may be achieved among them in the enjoyment of worldly goods. This one needs that one, this one makes for that one, and this one gives to that one.

As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "We subjected" means "We gave them servants and attendants, so that the rich employ the poor, and thus some of them become a means of livelihood for others." Qatadah and ad-Dahhak said: "so that some may possess others." It has also been said that السُّخْرِيّ (sukhriyy) here is the sense of "mockery" (istihza'). Although this matches the lexical meaning, it is far from the meaning of the Qur'an and contrary to the intended context.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾. By "mercy" is meant what Allah has prepared for His righteous servants in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is prophethood, since it is what is meant by "mercy" in the earlier words: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾. There is no barrier to meaning by it everything that is called "mercy", either by inclusion or by substitution (badal). The phrase مِمّا يَجْمَعُونَ (mimma yajma'un, "than what they accumulate") means: what they accumulate of wealth and all the other goods of this world.

Then He (glorified is He) explained the insignificance of this world in His sight, so He said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾, that is, were it not that they would all gather in disbelief out of inclination toward this world and its adornment, ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver ceilings for their houses﴾. He used the plural pronoun in لِبُيُوتِهِمْ (libuyutihim, "for their houses") and the singular in يَكْفُرُ (yakfuru, "disbelieves") with regard to the meaning and the wording of مَن (man, "whoever"). لِبُيُوتِهِمْ is a بَدَل اشْتِمال (badal ishtimal, a substitution of inclusion) from the relative pronoun. السُّقُفُ (suqufun, "ceilings") is the plural of سَقْفٌ (saqf, "ceiling").

The majority recited سُقُفًا with a ḍammah on the sīn and the qāf, like رَهْنٌ and رُهُنٌ. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "There is no third form like them." Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of سَقِيفٌ (saqif), like كَثِيبٌ and كُثُبٌ, and رَغِيفٌ and رُغُفٌ. It has also been said that it is the plural of سُقُوفٌ (suquf), so it is a plural of a plural. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited سَقْفًا with a fatḥah on the sīn and a sukūn on the qāf, in the singular, and its meaning is plural because it is a generic noun (li-l-jins).

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is: were it not that people would all disbelieve because of their inclination toward this world and their leaving the Hereafter, We would have given them in this world what We have described, because of the insignificance of this world in the sight of Allah. Most of the exegetes held this view.

Ibn Zayd said: "Were it not that mankind would become one community" means, in the pursuit of this world and their preference for it over the Hereafter.

Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is: were it not that among the disbelievers there were rich and poor, and among the Muslims there were the same, We would have given the disbelievers of this world all of this, because of its insignificance. ﴿And staircases on which they ascend﴾. (p-1340) The مَعارِج (ma'arij) are the stairs, the plural of مِعراج (mi'raj), and the mi'raj is the ladder.

Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may make the singular مِعْرَجًا (mi'rajan) and مَعْرَجًا (ma'rajan), like مِرْقاةٌ and مَرْقاةٌ. The meaning is: We would have made for them staircases of silver, upon which they ascend, that is, they climb and ascend by means of the staircases. It is said: ظَهَرْتُ عَلى البَيْتِ (zahartu 'ala al-bayt, "I ascended onto the house"), meaning I rose to its roof. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"We reached the heavens in glory, honour and lordship, and indeed we hope for a higher ascent beyond that."

That is, a place to ascend.

﴿And doors for their houses, and couches on which they recline﴾. That is, We would have made for their houses doors of silver and couches of silver, ﴿on which they recline﴾. That is, on the couches, which is the plural of سَرِيرٌ (sarir). It has also been said it is the plural of أَسِرَّةٌ (asirrah), so it is a plural of a plural. الِاتِّكاء (al-ittika') and التَّوَكُّؤ (tawakkus) mean leaning heavily upon something, as in ﴿I lean upon it﴾ [Taha: 18], and one says اتَّكَأ عَلى الشَّيْءِ (ittaka'a 'ala al-shay'), so he is مُتَّكِئٌ (muttaki'), and the place is مُتَّكَأٌ (muttaka'). The زُخْرُف (zukhruf) is gold. It has also been said that it is adornment in general, whether gold or otherwise. Ibn Zayd said: it is what people make for their homes of furnishings and household goods. Al-Hasan said: it is decorative designs, and its root meaning is adornment; one says زَخْرَفْتُ الدّارَ (zakhraftu al-dar, "I adorned the house"), meaning I decorated it.

The accusative of زُخْرُفًا (zukhrufan) is either by a verb understood, meaning: "and We would have made for them, in addition to all that, adornment", or by removal of the preposition, meaning: "doors and couches of silver and of gold", and when the preposition is removed, the noun becomes accusative.

Then He (glorified is He) informed that all of that is only enjoyed in this world, so He said: ﴿And all that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. The majority recited لَمّا (lamma) with a light pronunciation, while 'Asim, Hamzah and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited it with the doubled mīm (lammā). On the first reading, إنْ (in) is the light form of the heavy إنَّ, and on the second reading it is a negation, and لَمّا has the sense of إلّا (illa, "except"), meaning: "all that is nothing but a thing enjoyed in this world."

Abu Raja' recited لِمّا with a kasrah on the lām, on the basis that the lām indicates cause and مّا is a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted: that is, for that which is an enjoyment.

﴿But the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾. That is, for whoever guards against polytheism and sins, believes in Allah alone and acts in obedience to Him, for it is the enduring one that does not perish, and its everlasting bounty does not cease.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿We found our fathers upon a community﴾: "upon a religion."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him concerning ﴿And He made it a word that remains﴾: "There is no god but Allah" in his posterity, and he said: "The posterity of Ibrahim, his son."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him, that he was asked about the saying of Allah ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾ "What are the two towns?" He said: "al-Ta'if and Makkah." It was said: "Who are the two men?" He said: "'Umayr ibn Mas'ud, and the best of the Quraysh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him: "By the two towns is meant Makkah and al-Ta'if, and the great one is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Qurashi and Habib ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning the verse: "They mean: more honourable than Muhammad, [namely] al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from the people of Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from the people of al-Ta'if."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also concerning His saying ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾ and the rest of the verse: "He says: Were it not that We would make all mankind disbelievers, We would have made for the houses of the disbelievers ceilings of silver, and staircases of silver, which are steps upon which they ascend to the upper rooms, and couches of silver, and zukhruf, which is gold."

At-Tirmidhi related it and authenticated it, and Ibn Majah related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single drink of water from it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 36–45:

His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾. It is said: "I ʿashaw (aʿshū) toward the fire," meaning I headed toward it; and "I ʿashaw from it," meaning I turned away from it, just as you say "I ʿadaltu ilā fulān" and "ʿadaltu ʿanhu" (I inclined toward so-and-so and I inclined away from him), and "mintu ilayhi" and "mintu ʿanhu." So said al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, Abū al-Haytham and al-Azharī. The meaning, then, is: "And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful." Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning of the verse is that whoever turns away from the Qur'an and the wisdom in it, toward the falsehoods of those who lead astray, Allah punishes him with a devil whom He appoints for him, until it misguides him and stays with him as a companion, so he is not guided, as a recompense for him when he preferred falsehood over the clear truth.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿashw is a weak look. From it is the verse:

"How excellent a youth, you would gaze (taʿshū) toward the light of his fire, when the wind blows and the place is barren."

The apparent meaning of the line is the heading toward the fire, not looking at it with weak sight as al-Khalīl said, and this serves as evidence for what we mentioned earlier, that it comes with the meaning of heading toward and with the meaning of turning away. Likewise is what al-Khalīl cited as evidence for what he said, from the verse of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"Whenever you come to him, you gaze (taʿshū) toward the light of his fire, and you will find the best fire, and with it the best hearth."

The apparent meaning is: you head toward the light of his fire, not that you look at it with weak sight.

It may be said that the meaning in the two lines is hyperbole about the brightness and blaze of the fire, such that the onlooker sees it only as one whose sight is dimmed, due to the weakness that reaches his sight when he witnesses the magnitude of its fuel.

Abū ʿUbayda and al-Akhfash said: the meaning of ﴿And whoever ya-ʿshu﴾ is "and whoever his eye is darkened," which is similar to the saying of al-Khalīl. This is according to the reading of the majority: man yaʿshu, with a ḍammah on the shīn, from ʿashā yaʿshū.

Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah read "wa-man yaʿsha" with a fatḥah on the shīn. It is said: ʿashā al-rajul yaʿshā ʿashyan, when a man becomes blind. From it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

"She saw a man, absent of the two arrivals, of irregular form, blind (aʿshā) and afflicted."

Al-Jawharī said: al-ʿashā, with the alif maqṣūrah, is the verbal noun of al-aʿshā, who is one who cannot see at night and can see by day; the feminine is ʿashwāʾ.

It was also read "yaʿshū" with a wāw, on the basis that man is a relative pronoun not implying the meaning of a condition.

The majority read ﴿nuqayyiḍ lahu shayṭānan﴾ with the nūn. Al-Sulamī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, ʿIṣmah from ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿmash read it with the yāʾ, in the active voice. Ibn ʿAbbās read it with the yāʾ in the passive voice, with shayṭān raised as the deputy of the subject. ﴿Then he is for him a companion﴾, meaning: constantly attached to him, not separating from him; or he is constantly attached to the devil, not separating from him, but following him in all his affairs and obeying him in everything he whispers to him.

﴿And indeed they hinder them from the way﴾, meaning: and indeed the devils whom Allah appoints for every person who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, as is implied by ﴿la-yaṣuddūnahum﴾, that is: they come between them and the path of truth and prevent them from it, and whisper to them that they are upon guidance, until they think the truth of what they whisper; this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and they suppose that they are guided﴾, that is: the disbelievers suppose that the devils are guided, so they obey them; or the disbelievers, because of that whispering, suppose that they themselves are guided.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. The majority read it in the dual, that is, the disbeliever and the devil accompanying him. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafs read it in the singular, that is, the disbeliever; or each one of them comes, the disbeliever says to the devil, addressing him: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts﴾, that is, the distance between the east and the west, so the east was given precedence over the west.

Muqātil said: The disbeliever wishes that between them were the distance of the longest day's east from the shortest day's east in the year. The first is better, and al-Farrāʾ said so as well. ﴿Then how wretched is the companion﴾: the object of the dispraise is omitted, that is: you, O devil.

﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾. So said al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, Abū al-Haytham and al-Azharī. The meaning, then, is: "And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful." Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning of the verse is that whoever turns away from the Qur'an and the wisdom in it, toward the falsehoods of those who lead astray, Allah punishes him with a devil whom He appoints for him, until it misguides him and stays with him as a companion, so he is not guided, as a recompense for him when he preferred falsehood over the clear truth.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿashw is a weak look. From it is the verse:

"How excellent a youth, you would gaze (taʿshū) toward the light of his fire, when the wind blows and the place is barren."

The apparent meaning of the line is the heading toward the fire, not looking at it with weak sight as al-Khalīl said, and this serves as evidence for what we mentioned earlier, that it comes with the meaning of heading toward and with the meaning of turning away. Likewise is what al-Khalīl cited as evidence for what he said, from the verse of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"Whenever you come to him, you gaze (taʿshū) toward the light of his fire, and you will find the best fire, and with it the best hearth."

The apparent meaning is: you head toward the light of his fire, not that you look at it with weak sight.

It may be said that the meaning in the two lines is hyperbole about the brightness and blaze of the fire, such that the onlooker sees it only as one whose sight is dimmed, due to the weakness that reaches his sight when he witnesses the magnitude of its fuel.

Abū ʿUbayda and al-Akhfash said: the meaning of ﴿And whoever ya-ʿshu﴾ is "and whoever his eye is darkened," which is similar to the saying of al-Khalīl. This is according to the reading of the majority: man yaʿshu, with a ḍammah on the shīn, from ʿashā yaʿshū.

Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah read "wa-man yaʿsha" with a fatḥah on the shīn. It is said: ʿashā al-rajul yaʿshā ʿashyan, when a man becomes blind. From it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

"She saw a man, absent of the two arrivals, of irregular form, blind (aʿshā) and afflicted."

Al-Jawharī said: al-ʿashā, with the alif maqṣūrah, is the verbal noun of al-aʿshā, who is one who cannot see at night and can see by day; the feminine is ʿashwāʾ.

It was also read "yaʿshū" with a wāw, on the basis that man is a relative pronoun not implying the meaning of a condition.

The majority read ﴿nuqayyiḍ lahu shayṭānan﴾ with the nūn. Al-Sulamī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, ʿIṣmah from ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿmash read it with the yāʾ, in the active voice. ﴿And indeed they hinder them from the way﴾, meaning: and indeed the devils whom Allah appoints for every person who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, as is implied by ﴿la-yaṣuddūnahum﴾, that is: they come between them and the path of truth and prevent them from it, and whisper to them that they are upon guidance, until they think the truth of what they whisper; this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and they suppose that they are guided﴾, that is: the disbelievers suppose that the devils are guided, so they obey them; or the disbelievers, because of that whispering, suppose that they themselves are guided.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. The majority read it in the dual, that is, the disbeliever and the devil accompanying him. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafs read it in the singular, that is, the disbeliever; or each one of them comes, the disbeliever says to the devil, addressing him: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts﴾, that is, the distance between the east and the west, so the east was given precedence over the west.

﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾. This is a report of what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿since you wronged yourselves﴾, that is, on account of your wronging yourselves in the world. It was said that ʾidh is a substitute for "today," because it became clear on that day that they had wronged themselves in the world.

The majority read ﴿that you in the punishment are partners﴾ with the fatḥah on anna, on the basis that it and what follows are in a position of raising as the agent: that is, your partnership in the punishment will not benefit you today.

The exegetes said: no part of the punishment is lightened for them because of the partnership, since each one of the disbelievers and devils has the greatest share of it.

It is said: "I ʿashaw (aʿshū) toward the fire," meaning I headed toward it; and "I ʿashaw from it," meaning I turned away from it, just as you say "I ʿadaltu ilā fulān" and "ʿadaltu ʿanhu" (I inclined toward so-and-so and I inclined away from him), and "mintu ilayhi" and "mintu ʿanhu." So said al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, Abū al-Haytham and al-Azharī. The meaning, then, is: "And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful." Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning of the verse is that whoever turns away from the Qur'an and the wisdom in it, toward the falsehoods of those who lead astray, Allah punishes him with a devil whom He appoints for him, until it misguides him and stays with him as a companion, so he is not guided, as a recompense for him when he preferred falsehood over the clear truth.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿashw is a weak look. From it is the verse:

"How excellent a youth, you would gaze (taʿshū) toward the light of his fire, when the wind blows and the place is barren."

The apparent meaning of the line is the heading toward the fire, not looking at it with weak sight as al-Khalīl said, and this serves as evidence for what we mentioned earlier, that it comes with the meaning of heading toward and with the meaning of turning away. Likewise is what al-Khalīl cited as evidence for what he said, from the verse of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"Whenever you come to him, you gaze (taʿshū) toward the light of his fire, and you will find the best fire, and with it the best hearth."

The apparent meaning is: you head toward the light of his fire, not that you look at it with weak sight.

It may be said that the meaning in the two lines is hyperbole about the brightness and blaze of the fire, such that the onlooker sees it only as one whose sight is dimmed, due to the weakness that reaches his sight when he witnesses the magnitude of its fuel.

Abū ʿUbayda and al-Akhfash said: the meaning of ﴿And whoever ya-ʿshu﴾ is "and whoever his eye is darkened," which is similar to the saying of al-Khalīl. This is according to the reading of the majority: man yaʿshu, with a ḍammah on the shīn, from ʿashā yaʿshū.

Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah read "wa-man yaʿsha" with a fatḥah on the shīn. It is said: ʿashā al-rajul yaʿshā ʿashyan, when a man becomes blind. From it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

"She saw a man, absent of the two arrivals, of irregular form, blind (aʿshā) and afflicted."

Al-Jawharī said: al-ʿashā, with the alif maqṣūrah, is the verbal noun of al-aʿshā, who is one who cannot see at night and can see by day; the feminine is ʿashwāʾ.

It was also read "yaʿshū" with a wāw, on the basis that man is a relative pronoun not implying the meaning of a condition.

The majority read ﴿nuqayyiḍ lahu shayṭānan﴾ with the nūn. Al-Sulamī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, ʿIṣmah from ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿmash read it with the yāʾ, in the active voice. Ibn ʿAbbās read it with the yāʾ in the passive voice, with shayṭān raised as the deputy of the subject. ﴿Then he is for him a companion﴾, meaning: constantly attached to him, not separating from him; or he is constantly attached to the devil, not separating from him, but following him in all his affairs and obeying him in everything he whispers to him.

﴿And indeed they hinder them from the way﴾, meaning: and indeed the devils whom Allah appoints for every person who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, as is implied by ﴿la-yaṣuddūnahum﴾, that is: they come between them and the path of truth and prevent them from it, and whisper to them that they are upon guidance, until they think the truth of what they whisper; this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and they suppose that they are guided﴾, that is: the disbelievers suppose that the devils are guided, so they obey them; or the disbelievers, because of that whispering, suppose that they themselves are guided.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. The majority read it in the dual, that is, the disbeliever and the devil accompanying him. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafs read it in the singular, that is, the disbeliever; or each one of them comes, the disbeliever says to the devil, addressing him: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts﴾, that is, the distance between the east and the west, so the east was given precedence over the west.

Muqātil said: The disbeliever wishes that between them were the distance of the longest day's east from the shortest day's east in the year. The first is better, and al-Farrāʾ said so as well. ﴿Then how wretched is the companion﴾: the object of the dispraise is omitted, that is: you, O devil.

﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾. This is a report of what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿since you wronged yourselves﴾, that is, on account of your wronging yourselves in the world. It was said that ʾidh is a substitute for "today," because it became clear on that day that they had wronged themselves in the world.

The majority read ﴿that you in the punishment are partners﴾ with the fatḥah on anna, on the basis that it and what follows are in a position of raising as the agent: that is, your partnership in the punishment will not benefit you today.

The exegetes said: no part of the punishment is lightened for them because of the partnership, since each one of the disbelievers and devils has the greatest share of it.

It was said: it is for the causal explanation of the negation of benefit, that is, because it is your right that you and your companions be partners in the punishment, just as you were partners in its cause in the world. This meaning is strengthened by the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, according to a difference reported from him, with a kasrah on inna.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that the call and the admonition do not benefit those for whom wretchedness has preceded: ﴿Then, are you going to make the deaf hear, or guide the blind?﴾. The hamzah is for the denial of wonder, that is: this is not for you; so let your breast not be constricted if they disbelieve. In it is consolation for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and information to him that none is able to do that except Allah, mighty and majestic. His saying: ﴿and whoever is in manifest error﴾ is coordinated with "the blind," that is: you do not guide whoever is like that. The meaning of the verse: these disbelievers are in the position of the deaf who do not understand what you have brought, and in the position of the blind who do not see it, because of their excessiveness in misguidance and their entrenchment in ignorance.

﴿And either We take you away﴾, by death before the punishment descends upon them, ﴿then indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾, either in the world or in the Hereafter. It was said: the meaning is: We will expel you from Makkah.

﴿Or We show you that which We promised them﴾ of punishment before your death, ﴿for indeed We are over them omnipotent﴾, whenever We wish We punish them.

Many of the exegetes said: Allah indeed showed him that on the day of Badr. al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: it concerns the people of Islam, meaning the trials that occurred after the Prophet ﷺ; there was after the Prophet ﷺ a severe trial, but Allah honored His Prophet ﷺ and did not show him any of that in his community. The first is better.

﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you﴾, that is, of the Qur'an, even if whoever denies it denies it. ﴿Indeed you are upon a straight path﴾, that is, a clear way. The clause is a reason for His saying: "so hold fast."

﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, that is: indeed the Qur'an is an honor for you and for your people, the Quraysh, since it was revealed to you while you are of them, in your language and their language. Similar is His saying: ﴿We have indeed sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 10]. It was said: it is an explanation for you and for your community in what you need. It was said: a reminder by which you remember the matter of the religion and act upon it. ﴿And you will be questioned﴾ about what Allah has made for you of honor. So said al-Zajjāj, al-Kalbī and others. It was said: they will be asked about what is binding upon them of standing by it and acting upon it.

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ Al-Zuhrī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: Jibrīl said that to the Prophet ﷺ when he was taken on the Night Journey. So the intended meaning is asking the prophets at that time when he met them, and this is said by a group of the early scholars.

Al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjāj and a group of scholars said: the meaning is: ask the nations of those whom We sent. This is said by Mujāhid, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan. The meaning of the verse on both views: their being asked whether Allah permitted the worship of idols in any religion of the religions, and whether that was permitted for any of them. The purpose is to rebuke the polytheists of Quraysh: what they are upon did not come in any of the sharīʿahs.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Makhzūmī that "Quraysh said: Appoint for every man among the companions of Muhammad a man to seize him. So they appointed Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allah for Abū Bakr, and he came to him while he was among the people. Abū Bakr said: To what do you invite me? He said: I invite you to the worship of al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā. Abū Bakr said: What is al-Lāt? He said: The children of Allah. He said: And what is al-ʿUzzā? He said: The daughters of Allah. Abū Bakr said: Then who is their mother? Ṭalḥah was silent and did not answer him. So he said to his companions: Answer the man. The people were silent. Then Ṭalḥah said: Stand up, O Abū Bakr, I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. So Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, the verse." And it is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and elsewhere that with every person there is a companion from the jinn.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAlī concerning His saying: ﴿Then either We take you away﴾, he said: His Prophet ﷺ departed, and His vengeance remained upon his enemy.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿Or We show you that which We promised them﴾, he said: the Day of Badr.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab reported through a chain from him concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: an honor for you and for your people.

Ibn ʿAdī and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās, both said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to present himself to the tribes in Makkah and promise them dominance. When they said: To whom will the kingship belong after you? He would remain silent and not answer them with anything, because he had not been commanded in that regard until ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ was revealed. After that, when he was asked, he would say: It is for Quraysh; but they did not answer him, until the Anṣār accepted him on that basis."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported through the chain of al-Kalbī from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, he said: Ask those to whom We sent messengers before you.

﴿Or We show you that which We promised them﴾ of punishment before your death, ﴿for indeed We are over them omnipotent﴾, whenever We wish We punish them.

Many of the exegetes said: Allah indeed showed him that on the day of Badr. al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: it concerns the people of Islam, meaning the trials that occurred after the Prophet ﷺ; there was after the Prophet ﷺ a severe trial, but Allah honored His Prophet ﷺ and did not show him any of that in his community. The first is better.

﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you﴾, that is, of the Qur'an, even if whoever denies it denies it. ﴿Indeed you are upon a straight path﴾, that is, a clear way. The clause is a reason for His saying: "so hold fast."

﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, that is: indeed the Qur'an is an honor for you and for your people, the Quraysh, since it was revealed to you while you are of them, in your language and their language. Similar is His saying: ﴿We have indeed sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 10]. It was said: it is an explanation for you and for your community in what you need. It was said: a reminder by which you remember the matter of the religion and act upon it. ﴿And you will be questioned﴾ about what Allah has made for you of honor. So said al-Zajjāj, al-Kalbī and others. It was said: they will be asked about what is binding upon them of standing by it and acting upon it.

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ Al-Zuhrī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: Jibrīl said that to the Prophet ﷺ when he was taken on the Night Journey. So the intended meaning is asking the prophets at that time when he met them, and this is said by a group of the early scholars.

Al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjāj and a group of scholars said: the meaning is: ask the nations of those whom We sent. This is said by Mujāhid, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan. The meaning of the verse on both views: their being asked whether Allah permitted the worship of idols in any religion of the religions, and whether that was permitted for any of them. The purpose is to rebuke the polytheists of Quraysh: what they are upon did not come in any of the sharīʿahs.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Makhzūmī that "Quraysh said: Appoint for every man among the companions of Muhammad a man to seize him. So they appointed Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allah for Abū Bakr, and he came to him while he was among the people. Abū Bakr said: To what do you invite me? He said: I invite you to the worship of al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā. Abū Bakr said: What is al-Lāt? He said: The children of Allah. He said: And what is al-ʿUzzā? He said: The daughters of Allah. Abū Bakr said: Then who is their mother? Ṭalḥah was silent and did not answer him. So he said to his companions: Answer the man. The people were silent. Then Ṭalḥah said: Stand up, O Abū Bakr, I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. So Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, the verse." And it is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and elsewhere that with every person there is a companion from the jinn.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAlī concerning His saying: ﴿Then either We take you away﴾, he said: His Prophet ﷺ departed, and His vengeance remained upon his enemy.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿Or We show you that which We promised them﴾, he said: the Day of Badr.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab reported through a chain from him concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: an honor for you and for your people.

Ibn ʿAdī and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās, both said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to present himself to the tribes in Makkah and promise them dominance. When they said: To whom will the kingship belong after you? He would remain silent and not answer them with anything, because he had not been commanded in that regard until ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ was revealed. After that, when he was asked, he would say: It is for Quraysh; but they did not answer him, until the Anṣār accepted him on that basis."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported through the chain of al-Kalbī from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, he said: Ask those to whom We sent messengers before you.

When Allah, glory be to Him, informed His Prophet that He would take vengeance on his enemy for him, and mentioned the agreement of the prophets on monotheism, He followed this with the account of Musa and Fir'awn, and an explanation of the punishment that befell Fir'awn and his people. So He said: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs whose explanation has already passed, ﴿to Fir'awn and his chiefs﴾. The *mala'* are the notables. ﴿So he said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"﴾, sent to you.

﴿But when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them﴾, mocking and ridiculing them. The answer to *lamma* (when) is *idha* (the sudden *idha*, indicating immediacy), because the implied meaning is: they were suddenly, at the time of their laughing, [caught in that state].

﴿And We did not show them a sign except that it was greater than its sister﴾. That is, each one of Musa's signs was greater than what preceded it, and more important in rank, although the one before it was itself great. It was also said that the meaning is: the first sign implies knowledge, and the second implies knowledge, so when the second is added to the first, clarity increases. The "brotherhood" among the signs means that they are similar and proportionate in their indication of the truth of Musa's prophethood, as one says: "This is the companion of this," meaning: the two are counterparts in meaning. The clause ﴿except that it was greater than its sister﴾ is in the position of a genitive as a description of *ayah* (sign). It was also said: the meaning is that each of the signs, when considered alone, would make the observer think that it is greater than all the other signs. A similar statement is the saying of the poet:

*Whoever you meet among them, you will say, "I have met their chief,"*
*like the stars by which the night traveller is guided.*

﴿And We seized them with the punishment, so that they might return﴾. That is, because of their denial of those signs. The punishment is the one mentioned in His words: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and a shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf: 130], and so on. He, glory be to Him, made clear that the reason for seizing them with punishment was the hope that they would return.

When they witnessed what he brought them of clear signs and manifest proofs, they supposed that this was a kind of magic. ﴿And they said, "O magician!"﴾ They used to call the scholars *sahara* (magicians) and to honour and revere the magicians, and magic was not a term of blame among them.

Al-Zajjaj said: They addressed him with what he had been called among them, namely "the magician." ﴿Pray to your Lord for us, by what He has covenanted with you﴾, that is, by what you have told us of His covenant with you: that if we believe, the punishment will be removed from us. It was also said that the covenant means prophethood. It was also said that it means the granting of a supplication in general. ﴿Indeed we are guided﴾, that is: if the punishment that has come down upon us is removed, then we shall be guided in what is to come, and we shall believe in what you have brought.

﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: Musa prayed to his Lord, and He removed the punishment from them. When the punishment was removed from them, they were suddenly, at the time of their breaking the covenant that they had placed upon themselves regarding being guided, in that state. *Naks* means to break, to annul.

﴿And Fir'awn called out among his people﴾. It was said: when he saw those signs, he feared the people's inclination toward Musa, so he gathered them and called out with his voice among them, or he ordered a herald to proclaim with his words: ﴿O my people, do I not possess the kingdom of Egypt﴾, which no one disputes with me over, and no opponent opposes me in? ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾, that is, beneath my palace. What is meant is that they are the Nile. Qatadah said: the meaning is "flowing before me." Al-Hasan said: "flowing by my command," that is, flowing under my command. Al-Dahhak said: by the rivers he meant the commanders, leaders and tyrants, and that they march under his banner. It was also said that by the rivers he meant the wealth. The first view is the better.

The *waw* in "wa-hadhihi" (and these) is coordinating, joining it to "kingdom of Egypt." The verb *tajri* (flows) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance. The demonstrative noun is the subject, *al-anhar* (the rivers) is its adjective, *tajri* is its predicate, and the clause is in the position of accusative. ﴿Do you not then see?﴾, that is, this, and that you may infer from it the strength of my kingdom, the greatness of my rank, and Musa's weakness in opposing me.

﴿Or am I not better than this one who is contemptible﴾. *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* that is presumed to mean *bal* (rather), which indicates a shift, not the interrogative hamzah that indicates denial. That is: rather, I am better. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *am* has the meaning of *bal*, and the meaning is: Fir'awn said to his people: "Rather, I am better."

Al-Farra' said: if you wish, you may take it as a question introduced by *am*, because it is connected to a statement before it. It was also said that it is superfluous, and Abu Zayd related from the Arabs that they make *am* superfluous, and the meaning is: "I am better than this."

Al-Akhfash said: there is an omission in the speech, and the meaning is: "Do you not see? Or do you see?" Then he began and said: "I am better." This is related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh, similar to the view of al-Akhfash. This is supported by the fact that 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Ya'qub al-Hadrami paused upon *am* with the implied meaning "or do you see?", so the second part was omitted because the first indicates it. On this view, *am* would be connected, not disconnected. The first view is better. A similar example is the saying of the poet quoted by al-Farra':

*She appeared like the sun's horn in the splendour of the morning,*
*and her form, or are you, is more graceful in the eye.*

That is: rather, you are.

Al-Farra' related that some reciters read *a-ma ana khayr* (is it not that I am better), that is: "Am I not better than this one who is contemptible," that is, weak, despicable, humiliated in himself, without honour. ﴿And who can hardly express himself clearly﴾ because of the impediment in his tongue. Its explanation has already passed in Surat Ta-Ha.

﴿Why then are not bracelets of gold cast upon him﴾, that is: why is he not adorned with gold bracelets, if he were great? Among them, when they made a man their leader, they would adorn him with a gold bracelet and encircle his neck with a gold collar.

The majority read *asawiratun*, the plural of *asware*, which is the plural of *siwar* (bracelet). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the singular of *asawira*, *asawir* and *asawir* is *aswar*, which is a dialectal form of *siwar*.

Hafs read *asworatun* (with a different vowelling), the plural of *siwar*. Ubayy read *asawir*, and Ibn Mas'ud read *asawib*.

Mujahid said: when they made a man their leader, they would adorn him with two bracelets and encircle his neck with a gold collar, as a sign of his lordship.

﴿Or the angels came with him as a series﴾. This is conjoined to *ulqiya* (were cast), and the meaning is: why did the angels not come with him in succession, accompanying one another, if he were truthful, assisting him in his affair and bearing witness to his prophethood? So the accursed one led his people to think that messengers must be in the form of tyrants and surrounded by angels.

﴿So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him﴾, that is: he moved them to frivolity of ignorance and folly by his words, his deception and his delusion, so they obeyed him in what he commanded them, accepted it, and denied Musa. ﴿Indeed they were a corrupt people﴾, that is: they were outside the obedience of Allah.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the meaning is that he deemed his people ignorant, so they obeyed him through the lightness of their intellects and the scarcity of their reason. It is said: *istakhaffahu al-faraḥ* means "joy agitated him," and *istakhaffahu* means "carried him," and from this is His words: ﴿and let not those who have no certainty make you light﴾ [al-Rum: 60]. It was also said: he made his people light, that is, he found them light-minded, and he treated his people lightly and subdued them until they followed him.

﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. The commentators said: they angered us. *Asaf* means anger. It was also said: it is the intensest anger; it was also said: wrath. It was also said: the meaning is that they angered Our messengers.

Then He explained the punishment with which the vengeance fell upon them, saying: ﴿So We drowned them all﴾ in the sea.

﴿And We made them a precedent﴾, that is: an example for those among the disbelievers who act as they did, in deserving punishment.

The majority read *salafan* with a fatha on the *sin* and the *lam*, the plural of *salif*, like *khadam* and *khadim*, *rasad* and *rasid*, *haras* and *haris*. It is said: *salafa yaslufu* when one goes ahead and passes on.

'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqamah, Abu Wa'il, al-Nakha'i and Humayd ibn Qays read it with a damma on the *sin* and a fatha on the *lam*, the plural of *sulfah*, which is the advanced group, like *ghuraf* and *ghurfah*, as al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said. ﴿And an example for the later ones﴾, that is: a lesson and an admonition for those who come after them, or a wondrous story that serves as a proverb.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning ﴿when they angered Us﴾: he said: they provoked Us. They both also related from him, concerning *asafuna*: he said: they made Us angry. And concerning *salafan* he said: different desires.

And he recited: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all﴾.

Al-Farra' related that some reciters read *a-ma ana khayr* (is it not that I am better), that is: "Am I not better than this one who is contemptible," that is, weak, despicable, humiliated in himself, without honour. ﴿And who can hardly express himself clearly﴾ because of the impediment in his tongue. Its explanation has already passed in Surat Ta-Ha.

﴿Why then are not bracelets of gold cast upon him﴾, that is: why is he not adorned with gold bracelets, if he were great? Among them, when they made a man their leader, they would adorn him with a gold bracelet and encircle his neck with a gold collar.

The majority read *asawiratun*, the plural of *asware*, which is the plural of *siwar* (bracelet). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the singular of *asawira*, *asawir* and *asawir* is *aswar*, which is a dialectal form of *siwar*.

Hafs read *asworatun* (with a different vowelling), the plural of *siwar*. Ubayy read *asawir*, and Ibn Mas'ud read *asawib*.

Mujahid said: when they made a man their leader, they would adorn him with two bracelets and encircle his neck with a gold collar, as a sign of his lordship.

﴿Or the angels came with him as a series﴾. This is conjoined to *ulqiya* (were cast), and the meaning is: why did the angels not come with him in succession, accompanying one another, if he were truthful, assisting him in his affair and bearing witness to his prophethood? So the accursed one led his people to think that messengers must be in the form of tyrants and surrounded by angels.

﴿So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him﴾, that is: he moved them to frivolity of ignorance and folly by his words, his deception and his delusion, so they obeyed him in what he commanded them, accepted it, and denied Musa. ﴿Indeed they were a corrupt people﴾, that is: they were outside the obedience of Allah.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the meaning is that he deemed his people ignorant, so they obeyed him through the lightness of their intellects and the scarcity of their reason. It is said: *istakhaffahu al-faraḥ* means "joy agitated him," and *istakhaffahu* means "carried him," and from this is His words: ﴿and let not those who have no certainty make you light﴾ [al-Rum: 60]. It was also said: he made his people light, that is, he found them light-minded, and he treated his people lightly and subdued them until they followed him.

﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. The commentators said: they angered us. *Asaf* means anger. It was also said: it is the intensest anger; it was also said: wrath. It was also said: the meaning is that they angered Our messengers.

Then He explained the punishment with which the vengeance fell upon them, saying: ﴿So We drowned them all﴾ in the sea.

﴿And We made them a precedent﴾, that is: an example for those among the disbelievers who act as they did, in deserving punishment.

The majority read *salafan* with a fatha on the *sin* and the *lam*, the plural of *salif*, like *khadam* and *khadim*, *rasad* and *rasid*, *haras* and *haris*. It is said: *salafa yaslufu* when one goes ahead and passes on.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: We made them precursors so that others might take warning from them. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *sulufan* with a damma on the *sin* and the *lam*. Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of *salif*, like *sururun* and *sarir*. Abu Hatim said it is the plural of *salaf*, like *khashab* and *khushub*. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqamah, Abu Wa'il, al-Nakha'i and Humayd ibn Qays read it with a damma on the *sin* and a fatha on the *lam*, the plural of *sulfah*, which is the advanced group, like *ghuraf* and *ghurfah*, as al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said. ﴿And an example for the later ones﴾, that is: a lesson and an admonition for those who come after them, or a wondrous story that serves as a proverb.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and can hardly express himself clearly﴾: he said: Musa had a speech impediment in his tongue.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning ﴿when they angered Us﴾: he said: they provoked Us. They both also related from him, concerning *asafuna*: he said: they made Us angry. And concerning *salafan* he said: different desires.

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see Allah giving a servant what he wishes while he persists in his sins, then that is only a gradual leading (*istidraj*) from Him to him." And he recited: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: I was with 'Abdullah when the sudden death was mentioned in his presence, and he said: "It is a relief for the believer and a regret for the disbeliever." ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾.

When Allah, glory be to Him, informed His Prophet that He would take vengeance on his enemy for him, and mentioned the agreement of the prophets on monotheism, He followed this with the account of Musa and Fir'awn, and an explanation of the punishment that befell Fir'awn and his people. So He said: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs whose explanation has already passed, ﴿to Fir'awn and his chiefs﴾. The *mala'* are the notables. ﴿So he said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"﴾, sent to you.

﴿But when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them﴾, mocking and ridiculing them. The answer to *lamma* (when) is *idha* (the sudden *idha*, indicating immediacy), because the implied meaning is: they were suddenly, at the time of their laughing, [caught in that state].

﴿And We did not show them a sign except that it was greater than its sister﴾. That is, each one of Musa's signs was greater than what preceded it, and more important in rank, although the one before it was itself great. It was also said that the meaning is: the first sign implies knowledge, and the second implies knowledge, so when the second is added to the first, clarity increases. The "brotherhood" among the signs means that they are similar and proportionate in their indication of the truth of Musa's prophethood, as one says: "This is the companion of this," meaning: the two are counterparts in meaning. The clause ﴿except that it was greater than its sister﴾ is in the position of a genitive as a description of *ayah* (sign). It was also said: the meaning is that each of the signs, when considered alone, would make the observer think that it is greater than all the other signs. A similar statement is the saying of the poet:

*Whoever you meet among them, you will say, "I have met their chief,"*
*like the stars by which the night traveller is guided.*

﴿And We seized them with the punishment, so that they might return﴾. That is, because of their denial of those signs. The punishment is the one mentioned in His words: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and a shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf: 130], and so on. He, glory be to Him, made clear that the reason for seizing them with punishment was the hope that they would return.

When they witnessed what he brought them of clear signs and manifest proofs, they supposed that this was a kind of magic. ﴿And they said, "O magician!"﴾ They used to call the scholars *sahara* (magicians) and to honour and revere the magicians, and magic was not a term of blame among them.

Al-Zajjaj said: They addressed him with what he had been called among them, namely "the magician." ﴿Pray to your Lord for us, by what He has covenanted with you﴾, that is, by what you have told us of His covenant with you: that if we believe, the punishment will be removed from us. It was also said that the covenant means prophethood. It was also said that it means the granting of a supplication in general. ﴿Indeed we are guided﴾, that is: if the punishment that has come down upon us is removed, then we shall be guided in what is to come, and we shall believe in what you have brought.

﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: Musa prayed to his Lord, and He removed the punishment from them. When the punishment was removed from them, they were suddenly, at the time of their breaking the covenant that they had placed upon themselves regarding being guided, in that state. *Naks* means to break, to annul.

﴿And Fir'awn called out among his people﴾. It was said: when he saw those signs, he feared the people's inclination toward Musa, so he gathered them and called out with his voice among them, or he ordered a herald to proclaim with his words: ﴿O my people, do I not possess the kingdom of Egypt﴾, which no one disputes with me over, and no opponent opposes me in? ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾, that is, beneath my palace. What is meant is that they are the Nile. Qatadah said: the meaning is "flowing before me." Al-Hasan said: "flowing by my command," that is, flowing under my command. Al-Dahhak said: by the rivers he meant the commanders, leaders and tyrants, and that they march under his banner. It was also said that by the rivers he meant the wealth. The first view is the better.

The *waw* in "wa-hadhihi" (and these) is coordinating, joining it to "kingdom of Egypt." The verb *tajri* (flows) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance. The demonstrative noun is the subject, *al-anhar* (the rivers) is its adjective, *tajri* is its predicate, and the clause is in the position of accusative. ﴿Do you not then see?﴾, that is, this, and that you may infer from it the strength of my kingdom, the greatness of my rank, and Musa's weakness in opposing me.

﴿Or am I not better than this one who is contemptible﴾. *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* that is presumed to mean *bal* (rather), which indicates a shift, not the interrogative hamzah that indicates denial. That is: rather, I am better. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *am* has the meaning of *bal*, and the meaning is: Fir'awn said to his people: "Rather, I am better."

Al-Farra' said: if you wish, you may take it as a question introduced by *am*, because it is connected to a statement before it. It was also said that it is superfluous, and Abu Zayd related from the Arabs that they make *am* superfluous, and the meaning is: "I am better than this."

Al-Akhfash said: there is an omission in the speech, and the meaning is: "Do you not see? Or do you see?" Then he began and said: "I am better." This is related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh, similar to the view of al-Akhfash. This is supported by the fact that 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Ya'qub al-Hadrami paused upon *am* with the implied meaning "or do you see?", so the second part was omitted because the first indicates it. On this view, *am* would be connected, not disconnected. The first view is better. A similar example is the saying of the poet quoted by al-Farra':

*She appeared like the sun's horn in the splendour of the morning,*
*and her form, or are you, is more graceful in the eye.*

That is: rather, you are.

Al-Farra' related that some reciters read *a-ma ana khayr* (is it not that I am better), that is: "Am I not better than this one who is contemptible," that is, weak, despicable, humiliated in himself, without honour. ﴿And who can hardly express himself clearly﴾ because of the impediment in his tongue. Its explanation has already passed in Surat Ta-Ha.

﴿Why then are not bracelets of gold cast upon him﴾, that is: why is he not adorned with gold bracelets, if he were great? Among them, when they made a man their leader, they would adorn him with a gold bracelet and encircle his neck with a gold collar.

Hafs read *asworatun* (with a different vowelling), the plural of *siwar*. Ubayy read *asawir*, and Ibn Mas'ud read *asawib*.

Mujahid said: when they made a man their leader, they would adorn him with two bracelets and encircle his neck with a gold collar, as a sign of his lordship.

﴿Or the angels came with him as a series﴾. This is conjoined to *ulqiya* (were cast), and the meaning is: why did the angels not come with him in succession, accompanying one another, if he were truthful, assisting him in his affair and bearing witness to his prophethood? ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. The commentators said: they angered us. *Asaf* means anger. It was also said: it is the intensest anger; it was also said: wrath. It was also said: the meaning is that they angered Our messengers.
