It was also said: the meaning is that the origin of the Messiah without a father and his giving life to the dead is evidence for the soundness of the resurrection.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is preferable.

The majority read "la-ʿilm" in the form of a verbal noun, making the Messiah "knowledge" as an intensification of the knowledge that is attained by his coming upon his descent. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Qatadah, Malik ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a fatha on the ʿayn and the lam, meaning: his coming is a sign (ʿalam) among its signs and a condition among its conditions. Abu Nadrah and 'Ikrimah read "wa-innahu la-l-ʿalam" with two lams and a fatha on the ʿayn and lam, meaning: it is the sign by which the establishment of the Hour is known.

﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾, i.e., do not doubt its occurrence, nor deny it, for it will certainly come to pass. ﴿And follow Me; this is a straight path﴾, i.e., follow me in what I command you concerning monotheism and the nullity of polytheism, and the obligations of Allah which He has imposed upon you. This which I command you and call you to is a upright path that leads to the truth.

The majority read the omission of the yā' from "ittabiʿūn" both in pause and in continuation; likewise they read its omission in both states in "aṭīʿūn." Ya'qub read it with the yā' affirmed in both continuation and pause in both of them. Abu 'Amr, and a narration from Nafi', read it with the omission in continuation but not in pause.

﴿And let not Satan turn you away﴾, i.e., do not be deceived by his whisperings and his doubts which he casts into your hearts, so that they prevent you from following me, for what I call you to is the religion of Allah, upon which His messengers and His books agreed.

Then He explained the reason for their prohibition from being turned away by Satan by clarifying his enmity toward them, so He said: ﴿Indeed, he is to you an manifest enemy﴾, i.e., harmful, by his enmity toward you, not abstaining from that nor concealing it, as is shown by what occurred between him and Adam, and what he bound himself to, of misleading all the children of Adam except the sincere servants of Allah.

﴿And when Jesus came with clear proofs﴾, i.e., he came to the Children of Israel with clear miracles and laws.

Qatadah said: "the clear proofs" here means the Gospel. ﴿He said: I have come to you with wisdom﴾, i.e., prophethood. It was also said: the Gospel. It was also said: what encourages toward what is good and restrains from what is ugly. ﴿And to make clear to you some of that about which you differ﴾, from the rulings of the Torah.

Qatadah said: meaning the disagreement of the sects that split into factions concerning the matter of Jesus. Al-Zajjaj said: what Jesus brought in the Gospel is only some of that over which they differed, and so he clarified for them in other than the Gospel what they needed. It was also said: the Children of Israel differed after the death of Musa about matters of their religion. Abu 'Ubayda said: "some" here means "all," as in His saying: ﴿Some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. Muqatil said: it is like His saying: ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50], meaning: what was made lawful in the Gospel of what had been forbidden in the Torah, such as camel meat, fat of every animal, and hunting fish on the Sabbath. The lam in ﴿and to make clear to you﴾ is conjoined to an implied clause, as if he said: "I have come to you with wisdom, to teach it to you, and to make clear to you."

Then he commanded them to piety and obedience, so He said: ﴿So fear Allah﴾, i.e., beware of His disobedience, and ﴿obey me in what I command you concerning monotheism and the laws.﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾. This is an explanation of what he commanded them to obey him in. ﴿This is a straight path﴾, i.e., the worship of Allah alone and acting upon His laws.

﴿Then the factions differed among themselves﴾. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "the factions" are the People of the Book, from the Jews and the Christians. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: they are the sects of the Christians who differed concerning the matter of Jesus. Qatadah said: the meaning of "among themselves" is that they differed amongst themselves. It was also said: they differed among those to whom they were sent from the Jews and the Christians, and "the factions" are the groups that formed parties.

﴿So woe to those who wronged﴾ from these dissenters, and they are those who associated partners with Allah and did not act upon His laws, ﴿from the punishment of a painful Day﴾, i.e., its punishment is painful, and it is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Do they await only the Hour﴾, i.e., do these factions watch for and expect only the Hour ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾, i.e., unexpectedly, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, i.e., they are not aware of it. It was also said: the intended "factions" are those who formed parties against the Prophet (ﷺ) and denied him, and they are the ones meant by His saying: ﴿Do they await only the Hour?﴾ The first is preferable.

﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be, to one another, enemies﴾, i.e., the intimate friends in the world who loved one another therein, on the Day the Hour comes to them, ﴿will be enemies to one another﴾, i.e., some of them will be hostile to others, because the ties between them will have been severed, and each one of them will be occupied with himself, and they will find those matters in which they were friends to be causes of punishment, so they become enemies.

Then He excepted the God-fearing, so He said: ﴿except the righteous﴾, for they are friends in this world and the Hereafter, because they found that friendship which had been between them to be among the causes of good and reward, so their friendship remained in its state.

﴿O My servants, no fear will be upon you today, nor will you grieve﴾, i.e., it is said to these God-fearing ones who loved one another for Allah's sake by this statement, and at that their fear departs and their grief is lifted.

﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾. The relative pronoun may be an attribute of "My servants," or a substitution for it, or an appositive to it, or cut off from it in the accusative position as praise, or in the nominative position by inception, and its predicate is: ﴿Enter the Garden﴾, under the assumption: "It will be said to them: enter the Garden." The first is preferable, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Muqatil said: when the fear occurs on the Day of Resurrection, a caller will call out: "O My servants, no fear will be upon you." When they hear the call, the creatures will lift their heads, and it will be said: "Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims," so the people of idols will lower their heads, those who were not Muslims.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "yā 'ibādī" with the yā' affirmed and quiescent in both continuation and pause. Abu Bakr and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read it with the yā' affirmed and with a fatha in both states. The rest read it with its omission in both states.

﴿Enter the Garden, you and your spouses, rejoicing﴾. By "spouses" is meant their believing women; it was also said: their companions from among the believers; it was also said: their wives from the Houris of ample eyes. ﴿You will be made glad (tuḥbarūn)﴾, i.e., you will be honoured; it was also said: you will be made luxurious; it was also said: you will rejoice; it was also said: you will be gladdened; it was also said: you will be amazed; it was also said: you will take delight in hearing. The preferable interpretation of that is joy and gladness arising from honour and blessing.

﴿There will be circulated among them platters of gold﴾. Ṣiḥāf is the plural of ṣaḥfah, which is a wide, broad bowl. Al-Kisa'i said: the largest of bowls is the jafnah, then the qaṣʿah, which feeds ten people, then the ṣaḥfah, which feeds five, then the makīlah, which feeds two or three men. The meaning is that for them in the Garden there are foods which will be circulated among them in platters of gold, and for them therein are drinks which will be circulated among them in ﴿akwāb﴾, which is the plural of kūb.

Al-Jawhari said: the kūb is a cup without a handle, and its plural is akwāb. Al-A'sha said:

"Ṣarīfiyyah, of pleasant taste, with foam between kūb and dann."

Another said:

"Reclining, its doors clapping, a servant walks about with the kūb upon it."

Qatada said: *al-kub* is the round cup, short in neck and short in handle, and *al-ibriq* (ewer) is long in neck and long in handle. Al-Akhfash said: *al-akwab* are the ewers that have no spouts (*kharatim*). Qutrub said: they are the ewers that have no handles (*'uran*).

﴿And therein is what the souls desire, and what the eyes delight in.﴾ Most readers recite *tashtahi* (تَشْتَهِي). Nafi', Ibn Amir and Hafs recite *tashtahihi* (تَشْتَهِيهِ), with the pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, the relative word "what"). The meaning is: what the souls of the people of Paradise desire of the varieties of food, drink and the like, whatever the soul seeks and craves, whatever it may be; and what the eyes delight in, of all the pleasant things that they enjoy and wish to behold. One says: *ladha al-shay'u yaladhdhu ladhadhan wa ladhadhatan*, meaning "the thing became pleasant and he found pleasure in it." In the Mushaf of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it reads: *tashtahihi al-anfusu wa taludhdhuhu al-a'yunu* (تَشْتَهِيهِ الأنْفُسُ وتَلَذُّهُ الأعْيُنُ). ﴿And you therein are abiding.﴾ You will not die, nor will you be expelled from it.

﴿And that is the Garden which you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do.﴾ That is, it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: this statement, namely that it has come to you as inheritance passes to the heir, because of the righteous deeds you used to do in the world. The demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*, "that") is the subject (*mubtada'*); "the Garden" is its attribute (*sifa*); "which you have been made to inherit" is an attribute of "the Garden"; and the predicate (*khabar*) is "because of what you used to do." It has also been said that the predicate is the relative clause together with its complement (*silah*), but the first view is preferable.

﴿For you therein is abundant fruit﴾: "fruit" is well known, and it denotes all fruits, fresh and dry. That is, for them in the Garden, besides food and drink, there is abundant fruit of many kinds and sorts. ﴿Of which you eat﴾: the word "of" (*min*) is either partitive (*tab'idiyya*) or initial (*ibtida'iyya*). The prepositional phrase was placed first for the sake of the verse-ending rhyme (*fasila*).

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the Quraysh: "There is no one worshipped besides Allah in whom there is any good." They said: "Do you not claim that Jesus was a prophet and a righteous servant of Allah's servants, and yet the Christians worshipped him? If you are truthful, then he is like their gods." So Allah revealed: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it.﴾ I said: "What does *yasuddun* mean?" He said: "They cry out in protest." ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour.﴾ He said: "It is the coming down of Jesus son of Mary before the Day of Resurrection."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from Abu Umama who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No people went astray after being guided, while they were upon it, except that they were given to disputation." Then he recited this verse: ﴿They did not strike it for you except for argument﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]. Many hadiths have been reported condemning disputation in falsehood.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that the polytheists came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Tell us, those whom we worship besides Allah, where are they?" He said: "In the Fire." They said: "And the sun and the moon?" He said: "And the sun and the moon." They said: "And Jesus son of Mary?" He said: Allah said: ﴿He is but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel.﴾

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Musaddad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted through several chains from him, concerning His saying ﴿And indeed, it is a sign of the Hour﴾, that he said: "It is the coming down of Jesus before the Day of Resurrection." Al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (*marfu'*) report. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu Hurayra something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Sa'd ibn Mu'adh who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the ties of kinship will be severed, lineages will become few, and brotherhood will be gone, except the brotherhood in Allah. This is His saying: ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his *Targhib*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His saying ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ that he said: "There are two believing friends and two disbelieving friends. When one of the two believers dies, he is given the glad tidings of Paradise, and he mentions his friend and says: 'O Allah, my friend so-and-so used to command me to obey You and Your Messenger, to command me to good, and to forbid me from evil, and he informed me that I would meet You. O Allah, do not let him go astray after me until You show him what You showed me, and be pleased with him as You are pleased with me.' Then it is said to him: 'Go. If you knew what he has with Me, you would laugh much and weep little.' Then the other dies, and their spirits are joined together, and it is said: 'Let each of you praise the other.' Each one says to his companion: 'What a fine brother, what a fine companion, what a fine friend!' And when one of the two disbelievers dies, he is given the glad tidings of the Fire, and he mentions his friend and says: 'O Allah, my friend so-and-so used to command me to disobey You and Your Messenger, command me to evil, and forbid me from good, and he informed me that I would not meet You. O Allah, then do not guide him after me until You show him what You showed me, and be wrathful with him as You were wrathful with me.' Then the other dies, and their spirits are joined together, and it is said: 'Let each of you praise the other.' Each one of them says to his companion: 'What a wretched brother, what a wretched companion, what a wretched friend!'"

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas who said: *al-akwab* are jugs of silver.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is not one of you except that he has a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. The disbeliever inherits the dwelling of the believer in the Fire, and the believer inherits the dwelling of the disbeliever in Paradise. This is His saying: ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been made to inherit.﴾"

(p-1346)

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 74–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾ means the people of criminal disbelief (al-ijram al-kufriyya), as is indicated by their being mentioned in contrast to the believers, for whom God, glorified is He, mentioned what came before this: ﴿will abide eternally in the punishment of Hell﴾, the punishment never ceasing for them, ever.

﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning that punishment will not be eased for them. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And they will be in despair therein﴾, meaning they will be hopeless of salvation. It was also said: they will be silent with the silence of despair. The verification of its meaning has already passed in al-An'am.

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning We did not punish them without a sin, nor with more than what they deserve. ﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves, by the sins they committed.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read al-zalimin (الظّالِمِينَ) in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of kana, with the pronoun being a separating pronoun (damir fasl). Abu Zayd al-Nahwi read al-zalimun (الظّالِمُونَ) in the nominative, so that the pronoun is the subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of kana.

﴿And they will call out: "O Malik!"﴾, meaning the criminals will make this call. Malik is the keeper of the Fire.

The majority read Ya Malik (يا مالِكُ) without truncation (tarkhim, the shortening of a vocative). Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read Ya Mal (يا مالُ) with truncation.

﴿Let your Lord decree upon us﴾, meaning [a decree of] death. They sought intercession through Malik with God, glorified is He, that he would ask Him to decree death upon them so that they could rest from the punishment. ﴿He will say: "Indeed you will remain"﴾, meaning you will remain in the punishment. It was said that he remained silent in answering them for eighty years, then answered them with this reply. It was also said he remained silent toward them for a thousand years, and it was said a hundred years, and it was said forty years.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾. It is possible that this is from the speech of God, glorified is He, and it is possible that it is from the speech of Malik. The first is more apparent. The meaning is: We sent to you the messengers and revealed to them the scriptures, and they called you, but you did not accept and did not believe. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾, not accepting it. By "the truth" is meant everything God commanded through the tongues of His messengers and revealed in His books. It was also said that it refers specifically to the Qur'an. It was said that the meaning of "most of you" (aktharakum) is "all of you." It was also said that it means the leaders and chiefs, and whoever else is among their followers.

﴿Or have they decided a matter, then indeed We are decreeing﴾. Here "am" (أمْ) is the disconnected (munqati') one, which carries the meaning of "bal" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, i.e., "Rather, they have decided a matter."

In this there is a transition from the lamentation of the people of the Fire to the narration of what occurs from these [disbelievers]. Al-Ibram means perfecting and firmly establishing. It is said: "I firmly established the matter (abramtu al-shay'): I made it firm and perfected it," and "He made the rope firm (abram al-habl)" when he firmly twisted it. The meaning is: rather, they have plotted a scheme against the Prophet (ﷺ), so We will plot a scheme against them. This was said by Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones plotted against﴾ [al-Tur: 42]. It was also said that the meaning is: or have they decided a matter, then We are the ones who decide against them Our command of punishment. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation?﴾, meaning: rather, do they think that We do not hear what they conceal within themselves, or what they speak in secret in an empty place, or what they confer about among themselves? Yes, We hear that and act upon it. ﴿And Our messengers are with them, writing﴾, meaning the guardian angels (al-hafaza) are with them, writing down everything that issues from them of speech or deed. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is conjoined to the clause indicated by "bala" (yes).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to the disbelievers a statement that would impose the proof upon them and cut off the doubt they put forward. So He said: ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ The meaning is: if He had a son in your claim and according to your assumption, then I would be the first to worship God alone, because whoever worships God alone has already repelled the idea that He has a son. Thus said Ibn Qutayba.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: the meaning is "There was not for the Most Merciful a son," and His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a new statement. It was also said the meaning is: Say, O Muhammad, if it were established that God has a son, then I would be the first to worship this son whose existence you claim. But it is impossible that He has a son.

In this there is a negation of a son in the most eloquent manner, the most complete expression, and the finest style. This is what is apparent from the Qur'anic composition. Of this same kind is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. A similar example is a man's saying to one who debates with him: "If you establish what you say by proof, then I will be the first to believe in it and say it." Here the "in" (إنْ) in "in kana" is conditional. Ibn Jarir and others preferred this.

It was also said that the meaning of "al-'abidin" is "those who are disdainful (al-anifin) of worship." This is a strained interpretation for which there is no need. However, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Yamani read al-'abidin (العَبِدِينَ) without an alif. It is said: 'abida, ya'badu, 'abadan (with a fatha vowel on the middle letter) when he was disdainful and angry, so he is 'abid, and the noun is al-'abada, like al-anafa (disdain). Perhaps what led those who read this irregular and remote reading was the difficulty of the meaning of ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, though it is neither unlikely nor objectionable.

Al-Jawhari related from Abu Amr concerning His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ that it is from disdain and anger. Al-Mawardi related it from al-Kisa'i and Ibn Qutayba, and al-Farra' said the same. Likewise Ibn al-A'rabi said: the meaning of al-'abidin is the disdainful and angry ones. Abu Ubayda said: its meaning is the deniers (al-jahidin), and he related: "'abidani haqqi," meaning he denied me my right. They have cited as evidence for the meaning they mention the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Those are my bondsmen, so bring me their like, / and I am too disdainful to satirize Kulayb of Darim."

And also his saying:

"Those are people who, if they satirized me, I would satirize them, / and I am too disdainful that Kulayb of Darim should be satirized."

There is no doubt that 'abida and a'bada, meaning he was disdainful or angry, is established in the Arabic language, and the transmission of these imams is sufficient as proof. But to regard this in the Qur'an as a strained interpretation for which there is no need, and a clear distortion, is [mistaken].

Ibn 'Arafa has refuted what they said, saying: it is only said "'abada, ya'budu, fa-huwa 'abd" (the active participle being 'abd), and it is rarely said "'abid." The Qur'an does not come with the rare of the language or the irregular.

The majority read walad (وَلَدٌ) in the singular. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read wuld (وُلْدٌ), with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam.

﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, meaning: [God is exalted] in declaring Him free and holy above what they say of falsehood, that He has a son, and [above] what they invent against Him, glorified is He, which does not befit Him. If this is from the speech of God, glorified is He, then He has declared Himself free of what they said. If it is from the completion of the speech of His Messenger, whom He commanded to say it, then He commanded him to add to what he related of their false assumption the declaration of his Lord's transcendence and holiness.

﴿So leave them to plunge and play﴾, meaning: leave the disbelievers, since they were not guided by what you guided them to, and they did not respond to you in what you called them to. Let them plunge into their falsehoods and amuse themselves in their worldly life. ﴿Until they meet their day which they are promised﴾, and this is the Day of Resurrection. It was said it is the punishment in this world. It was said: this is abrogated (mansukh, meaning replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). It was said it is not abrogated, and it was only expressed in the form of a threat.

The majority read yulaqu (يُلاقُوا). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿until they meet (yalqawa)﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and a sukun on the lam, without an alif. This reading is related from Abu Amr.

﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾. The prepositional phrases in both places are connected to "God" (ilah), because it means "one worshipped" (ma'bud) or "one deserving of worship" (mustahiqq lil-'ibada). The meaning: He is the One who is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth, or He is deserving of worship in the heaven and of worship on the earth.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "ilah" in both places is in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "He who is in the heaven is God, and He who is on the earth is God." Its omission was made acceptable by the length of the sentence. He said: the meaning is based on the statement of His divinity, not on being located within them.

Qatada said: He is worshipped in the heaven and the earth. It was also said that "fi" (in) means "ala" (upon), i.e., He is capable over the heaven and the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71]. Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿He who is in the heaven is Allah and He who is on the earth is Allah﴾, by including in the proper name (al-'alam) the meaning of the derived noun (al-mushtaqq), so that the prepositional phrase is connected to it in this respect.

﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: the one perfect in wisdom, abundant in knowledge.

﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. "Tabaraka" is of the form taf'ala, from "al-barakah" (blessing), which is abundance of goods. By "what is between them" is meant the air and what is in it of living creatures. ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning the knowledge of the time at which it will occur. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, so He will recompense each person with what they deserve of good and evil. In this there is a severe warning.

The majority read turja'un (تُرْجَعُونَ) with the second person (ta'), while Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the third person (ya').

﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him will not possess intercession﴾, meaning those whom they invoke besides God, such as idols and the like, will not possess intercession with God, as they claim, that they intercede for them.

The majority read yad'una (يَدْعُونَ) with the ya', while al-Sulami and Ibn Wathhab read it with the ta'.

﴿Except those who testify to the truth﴾, meaning the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and they know, meaning they have knowledge and insight into what they testified to. The exception may be connected (muttasil, meaning it is of the same kind as what precedes it), and the meaning is: except those who testify to the truth, and they are al-Masih (Jesus), 'Uzayr (Ezra), and the angels, for they possess intercession for whoever deserves it. It was said that it is disconnected (munqati', meaning not of the same kind), and the meaning is: but those who testify to the truth, these will intercede for them. It is also permissible that the excepted item is omitted, i.e., they do not possess intercession for anyone except those who testify to the truth.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: the meaning of the verse is that these do not possess intercession except for those who testify to the truth and believe with knowledge and insight. Qatada said: they will not intercede for their worshippers, but they will intercede for whoever testifies to God's oneness. It was said: the axis of connection in this exception lies in taking "those whom they invoke" as general for everything worshipped besides God, while the axis of disconnection lies in taking it as specific to the idols.

﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "God"﴾. The lam (اللّامُ) is the introductory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam), preparing for an oath. The meaning: if you asked these polytheists who worship idols who created them, they would acknowledge and admit that their Creator is God, and they are unable to deny it or to refuse, because the matter is so manifest and clear. ﴿Then how are they deluded?﴾, meaning: how do they turn away from the worship of God to the worship of others, and divert from it despite this acknowledgment? For the one who acknowledges that God is his Creator, if he deliberately goes to an idol or an animal and worships it alongside God, or worships it alone, then he has worshipped some of God's creatures, and in this there is ignorance beyond measure.

It is said: afakahu, ya'fikuhu, ifkan (أفَكَهُ يَأْفِكُهُ إفْكًا), when he turned him and diverted him from something.

It was also said that the meaning is: (and if you asked al-Masih, 'Uzayr and the angels who created them, they would surely say, "God"), so how are these disbelievers deluded in taking them as gods? It was also said that the meaning is: and if you asked the worshippers and the worshipped all together.

The majority read wa-qilihi (وَقِيلَهُ) in the accusative, as a conjunction with the position (mahall) of "al-sa'a" (the Hour), as if it were said: indeed He knows the Hour and He knows His saying. Or it is conjoined to "sirrahum wa-najwahum" (their secret and their private conversation), meaning He knows their secret and their private conversation, and He knows His saying. Or it is conjoined to the omitted object of "yaktubuna" (they write), meaning they write that and they write His saying. Or it is conjoined to the omitted object of "ya'lamuna" (they know), meaning they know that and they know His saying. Or it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning He spoke His saying. Or it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, meaning: God knows the saying of His Messenger. Or it is conjoined to the position of "bil-haqq" (with the truth), meaning he testified to the truth and to His saying. Or it is in the accusative by omitting the particle of oath.

Among those who permitted the first possibility were al-Mubarrad and Ibn al-Anbari. Among those who permitted the second were al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. Among those who permitted the accusative as a verbal noun were also al-Farra' and al-Akhfash.

Hamzah and ʿĀsim read *wa-qīlihi* in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), as a conjunction onto the wording of *al-sāʿah* (the Hour), meaning: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and the knowledge of his *qīl* (saying)." *Al-qawl*, *al-qāl* and *al-qīl* have one meaning. Alternatively the *wāw* is an oath particle (li-l-qasam).

Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Abū Qilābah, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Hurmuz and Muslim ibn Jundub read *wa-qīluhu* in the nominative (bi-l-rafʿ), as a conjunction onto *ʿilmu al-sāʿah*, meaning: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and with Him is his *qīl*." Or it is a subject (ʿalā al-ibtidāʾ) whose predicate is the clause mentioned after it. Or its predicate is omitted, its estimate being "*wa-qīluhu kayta wa-kayta*" ("and his saying is such and such"), or "*wa-qīluhu masmūʿ*" ("and his saying is heard").

Abū ʿUbayd said: it is said, "I said a *qawl*, a *qīl* and a *qāl*." The pronoun in *wa-qīlihi* refers to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Qatādah said: "This is your Prophet complaining to his Lord about his people." It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messiah (ʿĪsā). On both views, the meaning is that he said, calling upon his Lord: ﴿O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe﴾ — those to whom You sent me.

Then, when he called upon his Lord with this, He answered him with His saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, disregard their call; ﴿and say, "Peace"﴾, that is, my affair is one of submission from you and of leaving you alone.

ʿAṭāʾ said: he intends forbearance until My judgment comes down, and its meaning is leaving them alone, as in His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 55].

Qatādah said: He commanded him to pardon them, then He commanded him to fight them, so pardon was abrogated (mansūkh) by the sword. It was also said: it is muḥkam (unabrogated). ﴿But soon you will know﴾ contains a severe threat and a great warning from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The majority read *yaʿlamūn* with the *yāʾ* (third person), while Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the *tāʾ* (second person). al-Farrāʾ said: *salām* is nominative, with an implied *ʿalaykum* ("upon you") understood.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth wa-l-Nushūr* related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿And they will call, "O Mālik"﴾, that he said: He will remain silent with them for a thousand years, then he will answer them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾

Ibn Jarīr related from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, who said: Three men were between the Kaʿbah and its curtains, two Qurashīs and a Thaqafī, or two Thaqafīs and a Qurashī. One of them said: "Do you think Allah hears our speech?" Another of them said: "If you speak aloud He hears, and if you speak in secret He does not hear." Then it was revealed: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations?﴾ — the verse.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ that he said: "If the Most Merciful had a son" — ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾. He said: "The witnesses (al-shāhidīn)."

Ibn Jarīr related from Zayd ibn Aslam regarding His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ that he said: "This is a known usage of the Arabic language: *in kāna hādhā al-amr qaṭṭ*," meaning: "if this matter ever was," that is, "it never was." Ibn Jarīr also related the like of it from Qatādah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 43, verses 74–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾ means the people of criminal disbelief (al-ijram al-kufriyya), as is indicated by their being mentioned in contrast to the believers, for whom God, glorified is He, mentioned what came before this: ﴿will abide eternally in the punishment of Hell﴾, the punishment never ceasing for them, ever.

﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning that punishment will not be eased for them. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And they will be in despair therein﴾, meaning they will be hopeless of salvation. It was also said: they will be silent with the silence of despair. The verification of its meaning has already passed in al-An'am.

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning We did not punish them without a sin, nor with more than what they deserve. ﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves, by the sins they committed.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read al-zalimin (الظّالِمِينَ) in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of kana, with the pronoun being a separating pronoun (damir fasl). Abu Zayd al-Nahwi read al-zalimun (الظّالِمُونَ) in the nominative, so that the pronoun is the subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of kana.

﴿And they will call out: "O Malik!"﴾, meaning the criminals will make this call. Malik is the keeper of the Fire.

The majority read Ya Malik (يا مالِكُ) without truncation (tarkhim, the shortening of a vocative). Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read Ya Mal (يا مالُ) with truncation.

﴿Let your Lord decree upon us﴾, meaning [a decree of] death. They sought intercession through Malik with God, glorified is He, that he would ask Him to decree death upon them so that they could rest from the punishment. ﴿He will say: "Indeed you will remain"﴾, meaning you will remain in the punishment. It was said that he remained silent in answering them for eighty years, then answered them with this reply. It was also said he remained silent toward them for a thousand years, and it was said a hundred years, and it was said forty years.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾. It is possible that this is from the speech of God, glorified is He, and it is possible that it is from the speech of Malik. The first is more apparent. The meaning is: We sent to you the messengers and revealed to them the scriptures, and they called you, but you did not accept and did not believe. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾, not accepting it. By "the truth" is meant everything God commanded through the tongues of His messengers and revealed in His books. It was also said that it refers specifically to the Qur'an. It was said that the meaning of "most of you" (aktharakum) is "all of you." It was also said that it means the leaders and chiefs, and whoever else is among their followers.

﴿Or have they decided a matter, then indeed We are decreeing﴾. Here "am" (أمْ) is the disconnected (munqati') one, which carries the meaning of "bal" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, i.e., "Rather, they have decided a matter."

In this there is a transition from the lamentation of the people of the Fire to the narration of what occurs from these [disbelievers]. Al-Ibram means perfecting and firmly establishing. It is said: "I firmly established the matter (abramtu al-shay'): I made it firm and perfected it," and "He made the rope firm (abram al-habl)" when he firmly twisted it. The meaning is: rather, they have plotted a scheme against the Prophet (ﷺ), so We will plot a scheme against them. This was said by Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones plotted against﴾ [al-Tur: 42]. It was also said that the meaning is: or have they decided a matter, then We are the ones who decide against them Our command of punishment. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation?﴾, meaning: rather, do they think that We do not hear what they conceal within themselves, or what they speak in secret in an empty place, or what they confer about among themselves? Yes, We hear that and act upon it. ﴿And Our messengers are with them, writing﴾, meaning the guardian angels (al-hafaza) are with them, writing down everything that issues from them of speech or deed. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is conjoined to the clause indicated by "bala" (yes).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to the disbelievers a statement that would impose the proof upon them and cut off the doubt they put forward. So He said: ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ The meaning is: if He had a son in your claim and according to your assumption, then I would be the first to worship God alone, because whoever worships God alone has already repelled the idea that He has a son. Thus said Ibn Qutayba.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: the meaning is "There was not for the Most Merciful a son," and His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a new statement. It was also said the meaning is: Say, O Muhammad, if it were established that God has a son, then I would be the first to worship this son whose existence you claim. But it is impossible that He has a son.

In this there is a negation of a son in the most eloquent manner, the most complete expression, and the finest style. This is what is apparent from the Qur'anic composition. Of this same kind is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. A similar example is a man's saying to one who debates with him: "If you establish what you say by proof, then I will be the first to believe in it and say it." Here the "in" (إنْ) in "in kana" is conditional. Ibn Jarir and others preferred this.

It was also said that the meaning of "al-'abidin" is "those who are disdainful (al-anifin) of worship." This is a strained interpretation for which there is no need. However, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Yamani read al-'abidin (العَبِدِينَ) without an alif. It is said: 'abida, ya'badu, 'abadan (with a fatha vowel on the middle letter) when he was disdainful and angry, so he is 'abid, and the noun is al-'abada, like al-anafa (disdain). Perhaps what led those who read this irregular and remote reading was the difficulty of the meaning of ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, though it is neither unlikely nor objectionable.

Al-Jawhari related from Abu Amr concerning His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ that it is from disdain and anger. Al-Mawardi related it from al-Kisa'i and Ibn Qutayba, and al-Farra' said the same. Likewise Ibn al-A'rabi said: the meaning of al-'abidin is the disdainful and angry ones. Abu Ubayda said: its meaning is the deniers (al-jahidin), and he related: "'abidani haqqi," meaning he denied me my right. They have cited as evidence for the meaning they mention the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Those are my bondsmen, so bring me their like, / and I am too disdainful to satirize Kulayb of Darim."

And also his saying:

"Those are people who, if they satirized me, I would satirize them, / and I am too disdainful that Kulayb of Darim should be satirized."

There is no doubt that 'abida and a'bada, meaning he was disdainful or angry, is established in the Arabic language, and the transmission of these imams is sufficient as proof. But to regard this in the Qur'an as a strained interpretation for which there is no need, and a clear distortion, is [mistaken].

Ibn 'Arafa has refuted what they said, saying: it is only said "'abada, ya'budu, fa-huwa 'abd" (the active participle being 'abd), and it is rarely said "'abid." The Qur'an does not come with the rare of the language or the irregular.

The majority read walad (وَلَدٌ) in the singular. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read wuld (وُلْدٌ), with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam.

﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, meaning: [God is exalted] in declaring Him free and holy above what they say of falsehood, that He has a son, and [above] what they invent against Him, glorified is He, which does not befit Him. If this is from the speech of God, glorified is He, then He has declared Himself free of what they said. If it is from the completion of the speech of His Messenger, whom He commanded to say it, then He commanded him to add to what he related of their false assumption the declaration of his Lord's transcendence and holiness.

﴿So leave them to plunge and play﴾, meaning: leave the disbelievers, since they were not guided by what you guided them to, and they did not respond to you in what you called them to. Let them plunge into their falsehoods and amuse themselves in their worldly life. ﴿Until they meet their day which they are promised﴾, and this is the Day of Resurrection. It was said it is the punishment in this world. It was said: this is abrogated (mansukh, meaning replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). It was said it is not abrogated, and it was only expressed in the form of a threat.

The majority read yulaqu (يُلاقُوا). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿until they meet (yalqawa)﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and a sukun on the lam, without an alif. This reading is related from Abu Amr.

﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾. The prepositional phrases in both places are connected to "God" (ilah), because it means "one worshipped" (ma'bud) or "one deserving of worship" (mustahiqq lil-'ibada). The meaning: He is the One who is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth, or He is deserving of worship in the heaven and of worship on the earth.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "ilah" in both places is in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "He who is in the heaven is God, and He who is on the earth is God." Its omission was made acceptable by the length of the sentence. He said: the meaning is based on the statement of His divinity, not on being located within them.

Qatada said: He is worshipped in the heaven and the earth. It was also said that "fi" (in) means "ala" (upon), i.e., He is capable over the heaven and the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71]. Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿He who is in the heaven is Allah and He who is on the earth is Allah﴾, by including in the proper name (al-'alam) the meaning of the derived noun (al-mushtaqq), so that the prepositional phrase is connected to it in this respect.

﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: the one perfect in wisdom, abundant in knowledge.

﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. "Tabaraka" is of the form taf'ala, from "al-barakah" (blessing), which is abundance of goods. By "what is between them" is meant the air and what is in it of living creatures. ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning the knowledge of the time at which it will occur. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, so He will recompense each person with what they deserve of good and evil. In this there is a severe warning.

The majority read turja'un (تُرْجَعُونَ) with the second person (ta'), while Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the third person (ya').

﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him will not possess intercession﴾, meaning those whom they invoke besides God, such as idols and the like, will not possess intercession with God, as they claim, that they intercede for them.

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning We did not punish them without a sin, nor with more than what they deserve. ﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves, by the sins they committed.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read al-zalimin (الظّالِمِينَ) in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of kana, with the pronoun being a separating pronoun (damir fasl). Abu Zayd al-Nahwi read al-zalimun (الظّالِمُونَ) in the nominative, so that the pronoun is the subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of kana.

﴿And they will call out: "O Malik!"﴾, meaning the criminals will make this call. Malik is the keeper of the Fire.

The majority read Ya Malik (يا مالِكُ) without truncation (tarkhim, the shortening of a vocative). Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read Ya Mal (يا مالُ) with truncation.

﴿Let your Lord decree upon us﴾, meaning [a decree of] death. They sought intercession through Malik with God, glorified is He, that he would ask Him to decree death upon them so that they could rest from the punishment. ﴿He will say: "Indeed you will remain"﴾, meaning you will remain in the punishment. It was said that he remained silent in answering them for eighty years, then answered them with this reply. It was also said he remained silent toward them for a thousand years, and it was said a hundred years, and it was said forty years.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾. It is possible that this is from the speech of God, glorified is He, and it is possible that it is from the speech of Malik. The first is more apparent. The meaning is: We sent to you the messengers and revealed to them the scriptures, and they called you, but you did not accept and did not believe. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾, not accepting it. By "the truth" is meant everything God commanded through the tongues of His messengers and revealed in His books. It was also said that it refers specifically to the Qur'an. It was said that the meaning of "most of you" (aktharakum) is "all of you." It was also said that it means the leaders and chiefs, and whoever else is among their followers.

﴿Or have they decided a matter, then indeed We are decreeing﴾. Here "am" (أمْ) is the disconnected (munqati') one, which carries the meaning of "bal" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, i.e., "Rather, they have decided a matter."

In this there is a transition from the lamentation of the people of the Fire to the narration of what occurs from these [disbelievers]. Al-Ibram means perfecting and firmly establishing. It is said: "I firmly established the matter (abramtu al-shay'): I made it firm and perfected it," and "He made the rope firm (abram al-habl)" when he firmly twisted it. The meaning is: rather, they have plotted a scheme against the Prophet (ﷺ), so We will plot a scheme against them. This was said by Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones plotted against﴾ [al-Tur: 42]. It was also said that the meaning is: or have they decided a matter, then We are the ones who decide against them Our command of punishment. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation?﴾, meaning: rather, do they think that We do not hear what they conceal within themselves, or what they speak in secret in an empty place, or what they confer about among themselves? Yes, We hear that and act upon it. ﴿And Our messengers are with them, writing﴾, meaning the guardian angels (al-hafaza) are with them, writing down everything that issues from them of speech or deed. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is conjoined to the clause indicated by "bala" (yes).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to the disbelievers a statement that would impose the proof upon them and cut off the doubt they put forward. So He said: ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ The meaning is: if He had a son in your claim and according to your assumption, then I would be the first to worship God alone, because whoever worships God alone has already repelled the idea that He has a son. Thus said Ibn Qutayba.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: the meaning is "There was not for the Most Merciful a son," and His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a new statement. It was also said the meaning is: Say, O Muhammad, if it were established that God has a son, then I would be the first to worship this son whose existence you claim. But it is impossible that He has a son.

In this there is a negation of a son in the most eloquent manner, the most complete expression, and the finest style. This is what is apparent from the Qur'anic composition. Of this same kind is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. A similar example is a man's saying to one who debates with him: "If you establish what you say by proof, then I will be the first to believe in it and say it." Here the "in" (إنْ) in "in kana" is conditional. Ibn Jarir and others preferred this.

It was also said that the meaning of "al-'abidin" is "those who are disdainful (al-anifin) of worship." This is a strained interpretation for which there is no need. However, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Yamani read al-'abidin (العَبِدِينَ) without an alif. It is said: 'abida, ya'badu, 'abadan (with a fatha vowel on the middle letter) when he was disdainful and angry, so he is 'abid, and the noun is al-'abada, like al-anafa (disdain). Perhaps what led those who read this irregular and remote reading was the difficulty of the meaning of ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, though it is neither unlikely nor objectionable.

Al-Jawhari related from Abu Amr concerning His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ that it is from disdain and anger. Al-Mawardi related it from al-Kisa'i and Ibn Qutayba, and al-Farra' said the same. Likewise Ibn al-A'rabi said: the meaning of al-'abidin is the disdainful and angry ones. Abu Ubayda said: its meaning is the deniers (al-jahidin), and he related: "'abidani haqqi," meaning he denied me my right. They have cited as evidence for the meaning they mention the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Those are my bondsmen, so bring me their like, / and I am too disdainful to satirize Kulayb of Darim."

And also his saying:

"Those are people who, if they satirized me, I would satirize them, / and I am too disdainful that Kulayb of Darim should be satirized."

There is no doubt that 'abida and a'bada, meaning he was disdainful or angry, is established in the Arabic language, and the transmission of these imams is sufficient as proof. But to regard this in the Qur'an as a strained interpretation for which there is no need, and a clear distortion, is [mistaken].

Ibn 'Arafa has refuted what they said, saying: it is only said "'abada, ya'budu, fa-huwa 'abd" (the active participle being 'abd), and it is rarely said "'abid." The Qur'an does not come with the rare of the language or the irregular.

The majority read walad (وَلَدٌ) in the singular. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read wuld (وُلْدٌ), with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam.

﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, meaning: [God is exalted] in declaring Him free and holy above what they say of falsehood, that He has a son, and [above] what they invent against Him, glorified is He, which does not befit Him. If this is from the speech of God, glorified is He, then He has declared Himself free of what they said. If it is from the completion of the speech of His Messenger, whom He commanded to say it, then He commanded him to add to what he related of their false assumption the declaration of his Lord's transcendence and holiness.

﴿So leave them to plunge and play﴾, meaning: leave the disbelievers, since they were not guided by what you guided them to, and they did not respond to you in what you called them to. Let them plunge into their falsehoods and amuse themselves in their worldly life. ﴿Until they meet their day which they are promised﴾, and this is the Day of Resurrection. It was said it is the punishment in this world. It was said: this is abrogated (mansukh, meaning replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). It was said it is not abrogated, and it was only expressed in the form of a threat.

The majority read yulaqu (يُلاقُوا). Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿until they meet (yalqawa)﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and a sukun on the lam, without an alif. This reading is related from Abu Amr.

﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾. The prepositional phrases in both places are connected to "God" (ilah), because it means "one worshipped" (ma'bud) or "one deserving of worship" (mustahiqq lil-'ibada). The meaning: He is the One who is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth, or He is deserving of worship in the heaven and of worship on the earth.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "ilah" in both places is in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "He who is in the heaven is God, and He who is on the earth is God." Its omission was made acceptable by the length of the sentence. He said: the meaning is based on the statement of His divinity, not on being located within them.

Qatada said: He is worshipped in the heaven and the earth. It was also said that "fi" (in) means "ala" (upon), i.e., He is capable over the heaven and the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71]. Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿He who is in the heaven is Allah and He who is on the earth is Allah﴾, by including in the proper name (al-'alam) the meaning of the derived noun (al-mushtaqq), so that the prepositional phrase is connected to it in this respect.

﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: the one perfect in wisdom, abundant in knowledge.

﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. "Tabaraka" is of the form taf'ala, from "al-barakah" (blessing), which is abundance of goods. By "what is between them" is meant the air and what is in it of living creatures. ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning the knowledge of the time at which it will occur. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, so He will recompense each person with what they deserve of good and evil. In this there is a severe warning.

The majority read turja'un (تُرْجَعُونَ) with the second person (ta'), while Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the third person (ya').

﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him will not possess intercession﴾, meaning those whom they invoke besides God, such as idols and the like, will not possess intercession with God, as they claim, that they intercede for them.

The majority read yad'una (يَدْعُونَ) with the ya', while al-Sulami and Ibn Wathhab read it with the ta'.

﴿Except those who testify to the truth﴾, meaning the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and they know, meaning they have knowledge and insight into what they testified to. The exception may be connected (muttasil, meaning it is of the same kind as what precedes it), and the meaning is: except those who testify to the truth, and they are al-Masih (Jesus), 'Uzayr (Ezra), and the angels, for they possess intercession for whoever deserves it. It was said that it is disconnected (munqati', meaning not of the same kind), and the meaning is: but those who testify to the truth, these will intercede for them. It is also permissible that the excepted item is omitted, i.e., they do not possess intercession for anyone except those who testify to the truth.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: the meaning of the verse is that these do not possess intercession except for those who testify to the truth and believe with knowledge and insight. Qatada said: they will not intercede for their worshippers, but they will intercede for whoever testifies to God's oneness. It was said: the axis of connection in this exception lies in taking "those whom they invoke" as general for everything worshipped besides God, while the axis of disconnection lies in taking it as specific to the idols.

﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "God"﴾. The lam (اللّامُ) is the introductory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam), preparing for an oath. The meaning: if you asked these polytheists who worship idols who created them, they would acknowledge and admit that their Creator is God, and they are unable to deny it or to refuse, because the matter is so manifest and clear. ﴿Then how are they deluded?﴾, meaning: how do they turn away from the worship of God to the worship of others, and divert from it despite this acknowledgment? For the one who acknowledges that God is his Creator, if he deliberately goes to an idol or an animal and worships it alongside God, or worships it alone, then he has worshipped some of God's creatures, and in this there is ignorance beyond measure.

It is said: afakahu, ya'fikuhu, ifkan (أفَكَهُ يَأْفِكُهُ إفْكًا), when he turned him and diverted him from something.

It was also said that the meaning is: (and if you asked al-Masih, 'Uzayr and the angels who created them, they would surely say, "God"), so how are these disbelievers deluded in taking them as gods? It was also said that the meaning is: and if you asked the worshippers and the worshipped all together.

The majority read wa-qilihi (وَقِيلَهُ) in the accusative, as a conjunction with the position (mahall) of "al-sa'a" (the Hour), as if it were said: indeed He knows the Hour and He knows His saying. Or it is conjoined to "sirrahum wa-najwahum" (their secret and their private conversation), meaning He knows their secret and their private conversation, and He knows His saying. Or it is conjoined to the omitted object of "yaktubuna" (they write), meaning they write that and they write His saying. Or it is conjoined to the omitted object of "ya'lamuna" (they know), meaning they know that and they know His saying. Or it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning He spoke His saying. Or it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, meaning: God knows the saying of His Messenger. Or it is conjoined to the position of "bil-haqq" (with the truth), meaning he testified to the truth and to His saying. Or it is in the accusative by omitting the particle of oath.

Among those who permitted the first possibility were al-Mubarrad and Ibn al-Anbari. Among those who permitted the second were al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. Among those who permitted the accusative as a verbal noun were also al-Farra' and al-Akhfash.

Hamzah and ʿĀsim read *wa-qīlihi* in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), as a conjunction onto the wording of *al-sāʿah* (the Hour), meaning: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and the knowledge of his *qīl* (saying)." *Al-qawl*, *al-qāl* and *al-qīl* have one meaning. Alternatively the *wāw* is an oath particle (li-l-qasam).

Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Abū Qilābah, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Hurmuz and Muslim ibn Jundub read *wa-qīluhu* in the nominative (bi-l-rafʿ), as a conjunction onto *ʿilmu al-sāʿah*, meaning: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and with Him is his *qīl*." Or it is a subject (ʿalā al-ibtidāʾ) whose predicate is the clause mentioned after it. Or its predicate is omitted, its estimate being "*wa-qīluhu kayta wa-kayta*" ("and his saying is such and such"), or "*wa-qīluhu masmūʿ*" ("and his saying is heard").

Abū ʿUbayd said: it is said, "I said a *qawl*, a *qīl* and a *qāl*." The pronoun in *wa-qīlihi* refers to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Qatādah said: "This is your Prophet complaining to his Lord about his people." It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messiah (ʿĪsā). On both views, the meaning is that he said, calling upon his Lord: ﴿O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe﴾ — those to whom You sent me.

Then, when he called upon his Lord with this, He answered him with His saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, disregard their call; ﴿and say, "Peace"﴾, that is, my affair is one of submission from you and of leaving you alone.

ʿAṭāʾ said: he intends forbearance until My judgment comes down, and its meaning is leaving them alone, as in His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 55].

Qatādah said: He commanded him to pardon them, then He commanded him to fight them, so pardon was abrogated (mansūkh) by the sword. It was also said: it is muḥkam (unabrogated). ﴿But soon you will know﴾ contains a severe threat and a great warning from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The majority read *yaʿlamūn* with the *yāʾ* (third person), while Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the *tāʾ* (second person). al-Farrāʾ said: *salām* is nominative, with an implied *ʿalaykum* ("upon you") understood.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth wa-l-Nushūr* related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿And they will call, "O Mālik"﴾, that he said: He will remain silent with them for a thousand years, then he will answer them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾

Ibn Jarīr related from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, who said: Three men were between the Kaʿbah and its curtains, two Qurashīs and a Thaqafī, or two Thaqafīs and a Qurashī. One of them said: "Do you think Allah hears our speech?" Another of them said: "If you speak aloud He hears, and if you speak in secret He does not hear." Then it was revealed: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations?﴾ — the verse.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ that he said: "If the Most Merciful had a son" — ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾. He said: "The witnesses (al-shāhidīn)."

Ibn Jarīr related from Zayd ibn Aslam regarding His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ that he said: "This is a known usage of the Arabic language: *in kāna hādhā al-amr qaṭṭ*," meaning: "if this matter ever was," that is, "it never was." Ibn Jarīr also related the like of it from Qatādah.
